discription:
A comprehensive set of terrain and raster analysis tools built on GDAL, designed for geomorphologists, cartographers, and spatial analysts.
The toolbox enables automatic derivation of slope (Slope), aspect (Aspect), and hillshade (Hillshade) from elevation rasters, as well as calculation of terrain metrics such as Roughness, TRI, and TPI.
It also supports distance and proximity mapping (Proximity) and raster refinement or repair (Fill NoData, Sieve, Near black).
Outputs include both single-band analytical rasters and multi-band visual products, making them suitable for visualization and modeling workflows.

Typical use cases:
- Generate slope, aspect, and hillshade layers from a DEM for topographic visualization.
- Fill elevation gaps and analyze surface roughness for hydrological or geomorphological modeling.
- Derive TPI/TRI indices to classify terrain units and integrate with land-use data.

Implementation notes: Built on the GDAL processing framework. Ensure CRS and NoData consistency; large rasters may require substantial memory.
Tags: DEM, slope, aspect, hillshade, interpolation, NoData repair

tools.name: Aspect
tools.description:
Generates an aspect map from any GDAL-supported elevation raster.
Aspect is the compass direction that a slope faces. The pixels will
have a value from 0-360° measured in degrees from north indicating the
azimuth.
On the northern hemisphere, the north side of slopes is often shaded
(small azimuth from 0°-90°), while the southern side receives more
solar radiation (higher azimuth from 180°-270°).
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL DEM utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdaldem.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Analysis`

tools.name: Color relief
tools.description:
Generates a color relief map from any GDAL-supported elevation raster.
Color reliefs can particularly be used to depict elevations.
The Algorithm outputs a 4-band raster with values computed from the
elevation and a text-based color configuration file.
By default, the colors between the given elevation values are blended
smoothly and the result is a nice colorized elevation raster.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL DEM utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdaldem.html>`_.

tools.name: Fill NoData
tools.description:
Fill raster regions with NoData values by interpolation from edges.
The values for the NoData regions are calculated by the surrounding
pixel values using inverse distance weighting.
After the interpolation a smoothing of the results takes place.
Input can be any GDAL-supported raster layer. This algorithm is
generally suitable for interpolating missing regions of fairly
continuously varying rasters (such as elevation models for instance).
It is also suitable for filling small holes and cracks in more
irregularly varying images (like airphotos).
It is generally not so great for interpolating a raster from sparse
point data.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL fillnodata utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdal_fillnodata.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Analysis`

tools.name: Grid (Linear)
tools.description:
The Linear method perform linear interpolation by computing a Delaunay
triangulation of the point cloud, finding in which triangle of the
triangulation the point is, and by doing linear interpolation from its
barycentric coordinates within the triangle.
If the point is not in any triangle, depending on the radius, the
algorithm will use the value of the nearest point or the NoData value.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL grid utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdal_grid.html>`_.

RADIUS.name: RADIUS
RADIUS.description: In case the point to be interpolated does not fit into a triangle of the Delaunay triangulation, use that maximum distance to search a nearest neighbour, or use NoData otherwise. If set to ``-1``, the search distance is infinite. If set to ``0``, NoData value will be used.

tools.name: Grid (Moving average)
tools.description:
The Moving Average is a simple data averaging algorithm.
It uses a moving window of elliptic form to search values and averages
all data points within the window.
Search ellipse can be rotated by specified angle, the center of
ellipse located at the grid node.
Also the minimum number of data points to average can be set, if there
are not enough points in window, the grid node considered empty and
will be filled with specified NoData value.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL grid utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdal_grid.html>`_.
.. seealso:: `GDAL grid tutorial <https://gdal.org/tutorials/gdal_grid_tut.html>`_

tools.name: Hillshade
tools.description:
Outputs a raster with a nice shaded relief effect.
It’s very useful for visualizing the terrain.
You can optionally specify the azimuth and altitude of the light
source, a vertical exaggeration factor and a scaling factor to account
for differences between vertical and horizontal units.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL DEM utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdaldem.html>`__ .
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Analysis`

tools.name: Near black
tools.description:
Converts nearly black/white borders to black.
This algorithm will scan an image and try to set all pixels that are
nearly or exactly black, white or one or more custom colors around the
collar to black or white.
This is often used to "fix up" lossy compressed airphotos so that
color pixels can be treated as transparent when mosaicking.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL nearblack utility <https://gdal.org/programs/nearblack.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Analysis`

NEAR.description: Select how far from black, white or custom colors the pixel values can be and still considered near black, white or custom color.

Target pixels are those in the source raster for which the raster

This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL proximity utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdal_proximity.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Analysis`

tools.name: Roughness
tools.description:
Outputs a single-band raster with values computed from the elevation.
Roughness is the degree of irregularity of the surface.
It's calculated by the largest inter-cell difference of a central
pixel and its surrounding cell.
The determination of the roughness plays a role in the analysis of
terrain elevation data, it's useful for calculations of the river
morphology, in climatology and physical geography in general.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL DEM utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdaldem.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Analysis`

discription:
A toolbox focused on raster format and band structure conversion, supporting data preparation, image compression, and raster–vector interoperability.
Core capabilities include format translation and export (Translate, gdal2xyz), color space conversion between RGB and PCT (RGB ⇄ PCT), band selection and rearrangement (Rearrange bands), and raster polygonization (Polygonize) for generating attribute-based vector polygons.
Ideal for standardizing raster inputs, building map-ready band combinations, or exporting classified rasters for downstream vector analysis.

Typical use cases:
- Convert true-color imagery to 8-bit paletted format for storage efficiency or fast rendering.
- Extract and reorder specific bands to build custom composite layers for mapping.
- Vectorize classified rasters for area statistics or thematic cartography.

Implementation notes: Maintain CRS alignment and pixel registration; note that palette conversion may introduce dithering artifacts.
Tags: format conversion, band rearrangement, PCT, RGB, vectorization, GeoTIFF

raster sharing a common pixel value. Each polygon is created with an
attribute indicating the pixel value of that polygon.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL polygonize utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdal_polygonize.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Conversion`

tools.name: RGB to PCT
tools.description:
Converts a 24 bit RGB image into a 8 bit paletted.
Computes an optimal pseudo-color table for the given RGB-image using a
median cut algorithm on a downsampled RGB histogram.
Then it converts the image into a pseudo-colored image using the color
table. This conversion utilizes Floyd-Steinberg dithering (error
diffusion) to maximize output image visual quality.
If you want to classify a raster map and want to reduce the number of
classes it can be helpful to downsample your image with this algorithm
before.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL rgb2pct utility <https://gdal.org/programs/rgb2pct.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Conversion`

NCOLORS.description: The number of colors the resulting image will contain. A value from 2-256 is possible.

OUTPUT.description: Specification of the output raster. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **file_output_types** :end-before: **end_file_output_types**

discription:
The Raster Extraction toolbox provides a suite of tools for extracting, clipping, and converting spatial information from raster datasets.
Built on GDAL utilities, it supports operations such as clipping rasters by extent or mask layer (Clip by extent / mask layer), generating contour lines (Contour) or contour polygons (Contour Polygons).
It serves as a core module for terrain analysis, thematic mapping, and spatial data preparation, enabling efficient conversion between raster and vector representations.

Key functionalities:
- **Clipping by extent or mask**: Extracts specific regions from raster data using rectangular extents or vector masks.
- **Contour extraction**: Automatically generates contour lines or polygons from elevation or DEM rasters.
- **Coordinate consistency and reprojection**: Ensures spatial alignment and CRS coherence during raster extraction.

Typical use cases:
- Clip DEMs to regional study areas to improve analysis efficiency.
- Extract climate or land cover rasters within administrative boundaries for thematic mapping.
- Generate contour lines from DEMs for topographic visualization or slope zone analysis.

Implementation notes: Based on GDAL warp and translate utilities; supports multithreading; ensure consistent projection and appropriate resolution for large datasets.
Tags: raster clipping, mask extraction, contour, DEM, terrain analysis, GDAL

discription:
A GDAL-based toolkit for raster data management, processing, and publishing, designed for GIS data managers, remote sensing analysts, and web mapping developers. Core capabilities include efficient data organization and mosaicking, advanced raster algebra and analysis, and end-to-end performance optimization for both desktop rendering and web deployment.

**Key Capabilities:**

- **Organize & Mosaic:** Combine multiple raster datasets by **physically merging (Merge)** them or **virtually stitching (Build virtual raster)**. Supports managing large image collections with **Tile index** and **Retile**.
- **Process & Analyze:** Perform custom map algebra using the powerful **Raster calculator**, enhance image resolution by fusing imagery with **Pansharpening**, or conduct professional **Viewshed** analysis.
- **Optimize & Publish:** Drastically accelerate desktop rendering by **building overviews (pyramids)**. Generate web-ready tiles with a single click using **gdal2tiles** for fast-loading, interactive maps in the browser.
- **Metadata:** Quickly retrieve detailed metadata from a dataset using **Raster information**.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Large-Scale Image Management:** Create a lossless virtual mosaic (VRT) from hundreds of drone images using `Build virtual raster`, then `Build overviews` on it for smooth browsing in desktop GIS without creating massive intermediate files.
- **Web Map Publishing:** Generate a standard-compliant web map tile cache from a final orthoimage or DEM using `gdal2tiles`. Simply upload the resulting directory to a web server to publish online.
- **Remote Sensing Analysis:** First, fuse a high-resolution panchromatic image with a multispectral one using `Pansharpening`, then compute a vegetation index (e.g., NDVI) on the resulting high-res color image with the `Raster calculator`.

**Implementation Notes:**
Prioritize using Virtual Rasters (VRT) for lossless, fast mosaic previews. When handling large datasets, always build overviews (pyramids) first to boost rendering performance. Before executing, ensure all input rasters for the Raster Calculator share the same CRS, extent, and resolution.

**Tags:**
Mosaic, VRT, Pyramids, Tiles, Web Map, Raster Calculator, Pansharpening, GDAL

tools.name: Build overviews (pyramids)
tools.description:
To speed up rendering time of raster layers overviews (pyramids) can
be created. Overviews are lower resolution copies of the data which
QGIS uses depending of the level of zoom.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL addo utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdaladdo.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Miscellaneous`

CLEAN.name: CLEAN
CLEAN.description: Removes existing overviews from the raster. By default these are not removed.

LEVELS.name: LEVELS
LEVELS.description: Defines the number of overview levels calculated by the original resolution of the input raster layer. By default 4 levels will be taken into consideration.

OUTPUT.label: Pyramidized
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Output raster layer with overviews

tools.name: Build virtual raster
tools.description:
Builds a VRT (Virtual Dataset) that is a mosaic of the list of input
GDAL-supported rasters.
With a mosaic you can merge several raster files.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL buildvrt utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdalbuildvrt.html>`_.
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Raster --> Miscellaneous`

RESOLUTION.description: The output resolution of the mosaic. By default the average resolution of the raster files will be chosen. Options: * 0 --- Average (``average``) * 1 --- Highest (``highest``) * 2 --- Lowest (``lowest``)

SEPARATE.name: SEPARATE
SEPARATE.description: With 'True' you can define that each raster file goes into a separated stacked band in the VRT band.

PROJ_DIFFERENCE.name: PROJ_DIFFERENCE
PROJ_DIFFERENCE.description: Allows that the output bands have different projections derived from the projection of the input raster layers.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specification of the output raster layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **file_output_types** :end-before: **end_file_output_types**

Options: * 0 --- Nearest Neighbour (``nearest``) * 1 --- Bilinear (2x2 kernel) (``bilinear``) * 2 --- Cubic (4x4 kernel) (``cubic``) * 3 --- Cubic B-Spline (4x4 kernel) (``cubicspline``) * 4 --- Lanczos (6x6 kernel) (``lanczos``) * 5 --- Average (``average``) * 6 --- Mode (``mode``)

tools.name: gdal2tiles
tools.description:
Generates a directory with small tiles and metadata, following the
`OSGeo Tile Map Service Specification <https://wiki.osgeo.org/wiki/Tile_Map_Service_Specification>`_.
See also the
`OpenGIS Web Map Tile Service Implementation Standard
<https://www.ogc.org/standards/wmts>`_.
Simple web pages with viewers based on Google Maps, OpenLayers and
Leaflet are generated as well.
To explore your maps on-line in the web browser, you only need to
upload the generated directory onto a web server.
This algorithm also creates the necessary metadata for Google Earth
(KML SuperOverlay), in case the supplied map uses ``EPSG:4326``
projection.
ESRI world files and embedded georeferencing is used during tile
generation, but you can publish a picture without proper
georeferencing too.
This algorithm is derived from the
`GDAL gdal2tiles utility <https://gdal.org/programs/gdal2tiles.html>`_.

discription:
A concise yet critical GDAL toolkit focused on handling the Spatial Reference System (CRS) of raster data. This toolbox provides core functionalities for **assigning, transforming, and extracting coordinate systems**, ensuring accurate alignment and interoperability of raster data across different geospatial environments. It is an essential tool for all GIS users and data engineers dealing with multi-source, multi-CRS datasets.

**Key Capabilities:**

- **Projection Transformation (Warp):** Use the robust **Warp (reproject)** tool to accurately transform a raster layer from one Coordinate Reference System (CRS) to another. Supports various resampling methods and output resolutions.
- **CRS Assignment (Assign projection):** Use the **Assign projection** tool to quickly define the correct CRS for raster datasets that are missing spatial references or have incorrect CRS metadata, enabling them to display correctly on the map.
- **Projection Metadata Extraction (Extract projection):** Extract the raster file's projection metadata and write it to a separate **World File (.wld)**, facilitating data exchange with other systems or software that do not support embedded projection information.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Multi-Source Data Alignment:** Batch process rasters from different sources (e.g., UTM-projected aerial photos and WGS84 satellite data) using `Warp (reproject)` to a single standard projection (e.g., Web Mercator) for accurate overlay analysis.
- **Fixing Undefined Projection:** When a legacy image fails to align correctly, use `Raster information` to verify its metadata, and then employ `Assign projection` to define the correct CRS, restoring its spatial location capability.

**Implementation Notes:**
`Warp (reproject)` is the core transformation tool, but it resamples pixel values and may introduce slight geometric distortion. Therefore, aim to complete reprojection early in the workflow. Select 'Nearest Neighbor' for categorical data and 'Bilinear' or 'Cubic Convolution' for continuous data (like DEMs). Note that `Assign projection` only modifies metadata and does not alter pixel geometry.

**Tags:**
CRS, Projection, Coordinate System, Reproject, Warp, GDAL

discription:
This toolbox provides a set of crucial GDAL/OGR utilities focused on **data format conversion** and the **transformation between vector and raster data models**. Whether you need to migrate vector data between different file types or switch data between vector and raster analysis environments, this toolset offers efficient and reliable solutions.

**Core Capabilities:**

- **Format Conversion (Convert format):** Utilize the powerful OGR `ogr2ogr` engine to convert any supported vector format (e.g., Shapefile, GeoJSON, KML, GPKG) into another format, with support for data filtering and manipulation during the process.
- **Vector to Rasterization:** Offers the core rasterization function to convert vector geometries (points, lines, and polygons) into a raster image with specified resolution and extent.
- **Raster Overwrite & Assignment:**
    - **Attribute-based Overwrite (Overwrite with attribute):** Map the attribute value of an overlapping vector feature onto the corresponding raster pixels.
    - **Fixed-Value Overwrite (Overwrite with fixed value):** Set the raster pixels within the vector overlay area to a single, fixed user-defined value.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Data Migration & Compatibility:** Convert all project Shapefiles into GeoPackage (GPKG) or GeoJSON format in one step to suit web application or modern GIS database requirements.
- **Creating Masks/Analysis Layers:**
    - Convert vector polygon data (e.g., land use classification) to raster format using `Rasterize (vector to raster)` to serve as a base layer for subsequent raster algebra operations.
    - Use `Rasterize (overwrite with fixed value)` to impose a vector Area of Interest (AOI) boundary onto an existing raster layer for clipping or defining a specific analysis zone.

**Implementation Notes:**
When performing format conversion, be aware of the limitations of the target format, such as field length and data type. For rasterization, the resolution and extent of the output raster are critical parameters that directly affect the accuracy and file size of the result. Rasterization is the essential bridge connecting vector and raster analysis for users performing complex map algebra.

**Tags:**
Vector to Raster, Rasterization, Format Conversion, OGR, GDAL, Overwrite, Data Migration

discription:
This toolbox provides a set of standard vector geometry processing functions based on OGR/GDAL, focusing on **spatial relationship manipulation, geometric shape modification, and data aggregation** of features. It offers spatial analysts a reliable and high-performance suite of tools for solving fundamental geospatial problems such as distance analysis, data clipping, and polygon merging.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Geometry Modification & Creation:** Create impact zones using standard **Buffer vectors** or **One side buffer** for lines; generate geometric structures and samples along line features with **Offset curve** and **Points along lines**.
- **Data Extraction & Clipping:** Supports precise clipping and extraction of vector data, either by a **rectangular extent (Clip vector by extent)** or a **mask layer (Clip vector by mask layer)**, to focus the analysis area.
- **Data Aggregation:** Utilize the **Dissolve** function to merge adjacent or overlapping geometric features based on shared attribute values, enabling data simplification and statistical aggregation.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Site Suitability Analysis:** Create a `One side buffer` for a proposed road or pipeline to analyze its impact on the environment on one specific side.
- **Data Simplification & Aggregation:** Use the `Dissolve` operation to merge adjacent area features with the same land-use type into a single, larger geographical region for cartographic simplification or macro-level statistics.
- **Data Preprocessing:** Use `Clip vector by mask layer` to crop a large regional vector dataset down to the project's Area of Interest (AOI), reducing data size and speeding up subsequent processing.

**Implementation Notes:**
`Dissolve` operations can be time-consuming when processing massive datasets; ensure the selected dissolve field is accurate. `Buffer` and `Clip` tools are wrappers of OGR `ogr2ogr`, offering good compatibility and performance. The direction of the `Offset curve` depends on the digitization direction of the line.

**Tags:**
Clip, Buffer, Dissolve, Geometry Processing, Spatial Analysis, OGR, GDAL

discription:
This toolbox is a collection of utility functions based on OGR/GDAL technology, focusing on **data management, database integration, and advanced data querying**. It provides a crucial bridge and set of tools for users who need to interact with PostgreSQL/PostGIS databases, execute SQL statements for data filtering, or construct virtual data sources.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Database Integration & Import:** Offers the functionality to directly **export vector layers to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database**, supporting both available and new connection settings for seamless integration between desktop GIS and professional spatial databases.
- **Advanced Data Querying:** Use the **Execute SQL** tool to run complex SQL queries (based on OGR SQL) on the source vector layer, efficiently performing data filtering, attribute joins, and data restructuring, with the result output as a new layer.
- **Data Management & Virtualization:** Create a virtual vector dataset (VRT) containing multiple layers using **Build virtual vector** to serve as a single input for other algorithms; use **Vector Information** to quickly extract and view detailed metadata for any OGR-supported data source.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Database Migration:** One-click import of all project vector data into a PostGIS database for centralized management and multi-user sharing.
- **Complex Data Filtering:** Use `Execute SQL` to run complex conditional queries, such as `SELECT * FROM layer WHERE (attribute_1 > 10 AND attribute_2 = 'Type A') OR geometry IS NULL`, exceeding the filtering capabilities of traditional GIS software.
- **Data Inspection:** Before processing large external datasets, quickly check the feature count, geometry type, CRS, and integrity using `Vector Information` to prevent errors in subsequent analysis.

**Implementation Notes:**
The power of the `Execute SQL` tool depends on the user's proficiency with OGR SQL or SQLite dialect. When importing to a PostGIS database, pay close attention to connection parameters and encoding settings. The VRT file created by `Build virtual vector` is only an XML description of metadata, not the geometry data itself, but it significantly simplifies the input for certain algorithms.

**Tags:**
SQL, PostGIS, Database, Virtual Vector, OGR, Data Import, Metadata

discription:
This toolbox provides a set of key utilities focused on data format conversion within the **Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) 3D Tiles ecosystem**. It primarily addresses interoperability between the legacy B3DM format and the modern GLTF/GLB format, as well as the integration of 3D model data back into a standard 2D/3D **vector GIS environment**.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **3D Model Format Upgrade:** Use the **Convert B3DM to GLTF** tool to transform the older `.B3DM` (Batched 3D Model) tile format into the more modern, versatile `.GLTF` or binary `.GLB` formats, ensuring compatibility and efficiency in current 3D rendering engines.
- **3D Data Integration:** Utilize the **Convert GLTF to vector features** tool to extract the geometric structures and attribute information contained within `.GLTF` or `.GLB` files and convert them into standard 2D/3D vector feature layers, facilitating spatial analysis and overlay operations within the GIS environment.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **3D Tiles Data Migration:** Batch convert older B3DM tiles used in Cesium or other 3D rendering applications to GLTF to benefit from newer rendering features and smaller file sizes.
- **Model-to-GIS Integration:** Quickly convert GLTF/GLB models exported from external modeling software (e.g., Blender, SketchUp) into GIS vector features (e.g., building footprints, tree points) for geo-localized attribute querying and spatial statistics.

**Implementation Notes:**
The B3DM to GLTF conversion helps improve rendering performance and reduce format dependency. The GLTF to vector conversion is a vital step for integrating 3D models into 2D GIS analysis workflows, with the resulting vector features retaining the model's geometry and metadata.

**Tags:**
3D Tiles, B3DM, GLTF, GLB, 3D Model, Format Conversion, OGC

discription:
This toolbox is a comprehensive set of native tools focused on the **visual representation, map layout output, and style asset management** of GIS data. It offers cartographers an efficient solution covering the entire workflow from data styling and design to batch atlas production and final PDF/image export.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Style Asset Management & Automation:** Supports **extracting and combining** style databases from a QGIS project, and automatically matching symbols to attribute values to **create categorized renderers** (e.g., `categorizeusingstyle`).
- **Feature Visual Optimization:** Provides **Topological coloring** to optimize color distinction for polygon maps, and calculates angles for **automatic alignment of point symbols to lines** to enhance map aesthetics.
- **Map Layout & Batch Export:** Focuses on the batch export of **Atlases** (supporting single/multi-file PDF and image), and allows for the export of single print layouts as final products, or the extraction of layout extent information.
- **Text & Annotation Handling:** Supports **extracting** rendered map **label** information and **transferring annotations** for layered management.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Automated Cartography:** Use **Align points to features** to automatically orient point symbols (e.g., street signs) with the nearest road, then utilize **Create categorized renderer** for one-click completion of complex categorized symbolization.
- **Professional Report Output:** After setting up the atlas, use the **Export atlas layout** series of tools to generate a single PDF map book containing all map sheets, and can **extract map extents** to create a map index layer.
- **Data Review:** Use **Topological coloring** to ensure no adjacent administrative areas share the same fill color.

**Implementation Notes:**
This toolbox is key to achieving **efficient, uniform, and automated cartography**. Style management supports importing and exporting XML style databases. The atlas export functionality allows dynamic adjustment of output map extents without modifying the layout itself.

**Tags:**
Cartography, Style, Symbol, Layout, Atlas, PDF, Topological Coloring, Annotation

tools.name: Align points to features
tools.description:
Calculates the rotation required to align point features with their nearest
feature from another reference layer. A new field is added to the output layer
which is filled with the angle (in degrees, clockwise) to the nearest reference
feature.
Optionally, the output layer's symbology can be set to automatically use the
calculated rotation field to rotate marker symbols.
If desired, a maximum distance to use when aligning points can be set,
to avoid aligning isolated points to distant features.
.. hint:: This algorithm is designed for use cases like aligning building
 point symbols to follow the nearest road direction.
of point features

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Point features to calculate the rotation for

REFERENCE_LAYER.name: REFERENCE_LAYER
REFERENCE_LAYER.description: Layer to find the closest feature from for rotation calculation

FIELD_NAME.name: FIELD_NAME
FIELD_NAME.description: Field in which to store the rotation value.

APPLY_SYMBOLOGY.name: APPLY_SYMBOLOGY
APPLY_SYMBOLOGY.description: Rotates the symbol marker of the features using the angle field value

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT

OUTPUT.label: Aligned layer
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The point layer appended with a rotation field. If loaded to QGIS, it is applied by default the input layer symbology, with a data-defined rotation of its marker symbol.

tools.name: Combine style databases
tools.description:
Combines multiple QGIS style databases into a single style database.
If items of the same type with the same name exist in different source
databases these will be renamed to have unique names in the output combined database.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisstylefromproject`

OBJECTS.name: OBJECTS
OBJECTS.description: Types of style items in the input databases you would like to put in the new database. These can be: * 0 --- :ref:`Symbols <edit_symbol>` * 1 --- :ref:`Color ramps <color-ramp>` * 2 --- :ref:`Text formats <text_format>` * 3 --- :ref:`Label settings <showlabels>`

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT

tools.name: Create categorized renderer from styles
tools.description:
Sets a vector layer's renderer to a categorized renderer using matching symbols
from a style database. If no style file is specified, symbols from the user's
current :ref:`symbol library <vector_symbol_library>` are used instead.
A specified expression or field is used to create categories for the renderer.
Each category is individually matched to the symbols which exist within
the specified QGIS XML style database. Whenever a matching symbol name is found,
the category's symbol will be set to this matched symbol.
If desired, outputs can also be tables containing lists of the categories which
could not be matched to symbols, and symbols which were not matched to categories.

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Vector layer to apply a categorized style to

tools.name: Topological coloring
tools.description:
Assigns a color index to polygon features in such a way that no adjacent polygons
share the same color index, whilst minimizing the number of colors required.
The algorithm allows choice of method to use when assigning colors.
A minimum number of colors can be specified if desired. The color index is saved
to a new attribute named **color_id**.
The following example shows the algorithm with four different colors chosen; as you
can see each color class has the same amount of features.
  Topological colors example

MIN_COLORS.name: MIN_COLORS
MIN_COLORS.description: The minimum number of colors to assign. Minimum 1, maximum 1000.

MIN_DISTANCE.name: MIN_DISTANCE
MIN_DISTANCE.description: Prevent nearby (but non-touching) features from being assigned equal colors. Minimum 0.0.

BALANCE.name: BALANCE
BALANCE.description: Options are: * 0 --- By feature count Attempts to assign colors so that the count of features assigned to each individual color index is balanced. * 1 --- By assigned area Assigns colors so that the total area of features assigned to each color is balanced. This mode can be useful to help avoid large features resulting in one of the colors appearing more dominant on a colored map. * 2 --- By distance between colors Assigns colors in order to maximize the distance between features of the same color. This mode helps to create a more uniform distribution of colors across a map.

discription:
This toolbox focuses on the persistent storage, spatial database integration, and advanced SQL querying of GIS data. It offers efficient, native solutions for users who need to migrate data to professional databases (PostgreSQL/PostGIS, SpatiaLite) or leverage the power of SQL language for low-level data manipulation.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Database Import & Integration:** Supports **exporting vector layers to PostgreSQL/PostGIS** and **SpatiaLite** databases, enabling seamless connection between desktop GIS and both enterprise and lightweight spatial databases.
- **Advanced SQL Query & Manipulation:** Provides the **PostgreSQL execute SQL** and **SpatiaLite execute SQL** tool series, allowing users to run custom SQL statements directly on the database connections for data modification, management, or advanced querying, with support for loading query results as new layers.
- **Data Packaging & Distribution:** Uses the **Package layers** tool to efficiently bundle multiple vector layers into a single, standard **GeoPackage** file for easy single-file storage, transfer, and distribution.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Data Sharing & Performance:** `Export to PostgreSQL` all project vector data to enable multi-user simultaneous editing and leverage database-level spatial indexes for enhanced query performance.
- **Database Maintenance & Querying:** Without leaving QGIS, run a `VACUUM` statement directly via **PostgreSQL execute SQL** for database optimization, or execute spatial SQL (like ST_Intersection) for advanced analysis and load the result onto the map.
- **Single-File Distribution:** Use `Package layers` to bundle analysis results and related layers into a unified `.gpkg` file for sharing with colleagues or clients.

**Implementation Notes:**
Operations in this toolbox act directly on the database backend; permissions and connection settings are critical. The SQL tools allow modifications to the layer itself (e.g., updating attributes or deleting features) and should be used with caution. GeoPackage (`.gpkg`) is the OGC standard and is recommended for data packaging and distribution.

**Tags:**
Database, SQL, PostGIS, SpatiaLite, GeoPackage, Data Import, Data Packaging

new relation is created.

OVERWRITE.name: OVERWRITE
OVERWRITE.description: If the specified table exists, setting this option to ``True`` will make sure that it is deleted and a new table will be created before the features are added. If this option is ``False`` and the table exists, the algorithm will throw an exception ("relation already exists").

CREATEINDEX.name: CREATEINDEX
CREATEINDEX.description: Specifies whether to create a spatial index or not

discription:
This toolbox is a utility collection focused on GPS tracks, waypoints, and route data, fully implemented using the industry-standard **GPSBabel** command-line tool. It provides users with a **data transfer bridge between devices and GIS**, as well as the ability to efficiently convert data between various GPS formats and the universal GPX standard.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Device Data Transfer:** Offers **Download GPS data from device** and **Upload GPS data to device** functionalities, allowing users to directly transfer data to or from GPS devices (e.g., Garmin, Magellan), standardized via the GPX format for interaction.
- **Format Conversion & Standardization:** Utilizes the **Convert GPS data** tool to transform various non-standard or proprietary GPS data file formats into the widely supported **GPX standard format** for GIS.
- **Feature Type Restructuring:** Use the **Convert GPX feature type** tool to transform feature types within a GPX file (e.g., converting waypoints to routes) for tailored analysis.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Field Data Collection:** Directly `Download GPS data` from a GPS device to quickly acquire field-collected waypoints and tracks, and load them into the GIS project.
- **Route Planning & Upload:** After planning a survey route in GIS, use `Upload GPS data to device` to transfer the GPX file to a handheld GPS device for navigation.
- **Legacy Data Compatibility:** Use `Convert GPS data` to transform proprietary formats (e.g., Garmin CRS/TRK/USR) exported from older devices or software into the standard GPX format, resolving data compatibility issues.

**Implementation Notes:**
This toolbox is based on GPSBabel, giving it a wide range of supported devices and formats. All device operations rely on GPSBabel's underlying drivers. GPX is the universal XML format for GPS data and is highly recommended as the standard format for internal GIS processing and storage.

**Tags:**
GPS, GPSBabel, GPX, Data Conversion, Device Upload, Data Download, Waypoints, Tracks

discription:
This toolbox provides a set of key utilities focused on **transforming discrete vector features into continuous raster surfaces**. By utilizing **interpolation** and **density estimation** techniques, users can create heatmaps and surface models from point and line data that reflect spatial distribution trends, value variations, or clustering levels.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Continuous Surface Creation:** Supports two classic interpolation algorithms: **Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW Interpolation)**, which weights point values by distance to create a smooth surface; and **TIN Interpolation**, which generates a non-smooth surface model based on a Delaunay Triangulated Irregular Network.
- **Density Trend Analysis:** Offers the **Heatmap (kernel density estimation)** tool to calculate and visualize the spatial clustering and **hotspots** of point features; and the **Line Density** tool to calculate and visualize the density of linear features (e.g., roads, rivers) within a circular neighborhood, suitable for infrastructure analysis.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Environmental/Meteorological Modeling:** Use **IDW Interpolation** to convert discrete temperature or precipitation measurements from weather stations into a continuous regional temperature/rainfall raster map.
- **Crime/Epidemic Analysis:** Utilize **Heatmap (kernel density estimation)** to identify and visualize **hotspot areas** and clustering patterns of crime incidents or disease outbreaks.
- **Infrastructure Assessment:** Use **Line Density** to calculate the density distribution of roads or pipelines within an urban area to assess the coverage of infrastructure.
- **Elevation Surface Creation:** Use **TIN Interpolation** to quickly generate an elevation raster and triangulation boundaries from elevation points (DEM sample points).

**Implementation Notes:**
The key to interpolation tools is selecting the appropriate algorithm and parameters. IDW is best suited for smoothly varying surfaces, while TIN is not ideal for extrapolation (outside the data range). Density estimation results heavily depend on the chosen search radius, and are commonly used to identify spatial patterns.

**Tags:**
Interpolation, IDW, TIN, Heatmap, Density, Kernel Density Estimation, Surface Modeling

tools.name: Heatmap (kernel density estimation)
tools.description:
Creates a density (heatmap) raster of an input point vector layer
using kernel density estimation.
The density is calculated based on the number of points in a location,
with larger numbers of clustered points resulting in larger values.
Heatmaps allow easy identification of *hotspots* and clustering of
points.

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Point vector layer to use for the heatmap

RADIUS.name: RADIUS
RADIUS.description: Heatmap search radius (or kernel bandwidth) in map units. The radius specifies the distance around a point at which the influence of the point will be felt. Larger values result in greater smoothing, but smaller values may show finer details and variation in point density.

PIXEL_SIZE.name: PIXEL_SIZE
PIXEL_SIZE.description: Pixel size of the output raster layer in layer units. In the GUI, the size can be specified by the number of rows (``Number of rows``) / columns (``Number of columns``) **or** the pixel size( ``Pixel Size X`` / ``Pixel Size Y``). Increasing the number of rows or columns will decrease the cell size and increase the file size of the output raster. The values in ``Rows``, ``Columns``, ``Pixel Size X`` and ``Pixel Size Y`` will be updated simultaneously - doubling the number of rows will double the number of columns, and the cell size will be halved. The extent of the output raster will remain the same (approximately).

KERNEL.name: KERNEL
KERNEL.description: Controls the rate at which the influence of a point decreases as the distance from the point increases. Different kernels decay at different rates, so a triweight kernel gives features greater weight for distances closer to the point then the Epanechnikov kernel does. Consequently, triweight results in “sharper” hotspots and Epanechnikov results in “smoother” hotspots. There are many shapes available (please see the `Wikipedia page <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_(statistics)#Kernel_functions_in_common_use>`_ for further information): * 0 --- Quartic * 1 --- Triangular * 2 --- Uniform * 3 --- Triweight * 4 --- Epanechnikov

OUTPUT_VALUE.name: OUTPUT_VALUE
OUTPUT_VALUE.description: Allow to change the values of the output heatmap raster. One of: * 0 --- Raw * 1 --- Scaled

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output raster layer with kernel density values. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **file_output_types** :end-before: **end_file_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Heatmap
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Raster layer with kernel density values

tools.name: IDW Interpolation
tools.description:
Generates an Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) interpolation of a point
vector layer.
Sample points are weighted during interpolation such that the
influence of one point relative to another declines with distance from
the unknown point you want to create.
The IDW interpolation method also has some disadvantages: the quality
of the interpolation result can decrease, if the distribution of
sample data points is uneven.
Furthermore, maximum and minimum values in the interpolated surface
can only occur at sample data points.

INTERPOLATION_DATA.name: INTERPOLATION_DATA
INTERPOLATION_DATA.description: Vector layer(s) and field(s) to use for the interpolation, coded in a string (see the ``ParameterInterpolationData`` class in :source:`InterpolationWidgets <python/plugins/processing/algs/qgis/ui/InterpolationWidgets.py>` for more details). The following GUI elements are provided to compose the interpolation data string: * **Vector layer** [vector: any] * **Interpolation attribute** [tablefield: numeric]: Attribute to use in the interpolation * **Use Z-coordinate for interpolation** [boolean]: Uses the layer's stored Z values ( For each of the added layer-field combinations, a type can be chosen: * :guilabel:`Points` * :guilabel:`Structured lines` * :guilabel:`Break lines` In the string, the layer-field elements are separated by ``'::|::'``. The sub-elements of the layer-field elements are separated by ``'::~::'``.

DISTANCE_COEFFICIENT.name: DISTANCE_COEFFICIENT
DISTANCE_COEFFICIENT.description: Sets the distance coefficient for the interpolation. Minimum: 0.0, maximum: 100.0.

EXTENT.name: EXTENT
EXTENT.description: Extent of the output raster layer. .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **extent_options** :end-before: **end_extent_options**

PIXEL_SIZE.name: PIXEL_SIZE
PIXEL_SIZE.description: Pixel size of the output raster layer in layer units. In the GUI, the size can be specified by the number of rows (``Number of rows``) / columns (``Number of columns``) **or** the pixel size( ``Pixel Size X`` / ``Pixel Size Y``). Increasing the number of rows or columns will decrease the cell size and increase the file size of the output raster. The values in ``Rows``, ``Columns``, ``Pixel Size X`` and ``Pixel Size Y`` will be updated simultaneously - doubling the number of rows will double the number of columns, and the cell size will be halved. The extent of the output raster will remain the same (approximately).

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Raster layer of interpolated values. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **file_output_types** :end-before: **end_file_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Interpolated
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Raster layer of interpolated values

tools.name: Line Density
tools.description:
Calculates for each raster cell, the density measure of linear
features within a circular neighbourhood. This measure is obtained by
summing all the line segments intersecting the circular neighbourhood
and dividing this sum by the area of such neighbourhood. 
A weighting factor can be applied to the line segments. 
  Line density example. Input layer source: Roads Overijssel - The
  Netherlands (OSM).

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Input vector layer containing line features

WEIGHT.name: WEIGHT
WEIGHT.description: Field of the layer containing the weight factor to use during the calculation

RADIUS.name: RADIUS
RADIUS.description: Radius of the circular neighbourhood. Units can be specified here.

PIXEL_SIZE.name: PIXEL_SIZE
PIXEL_SIZE.description: Pixel size of the output raster layer in layer units. The raster has square pixels.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output as a raster layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **file_output_types** :end-before: **end_file_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Line density raster
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output line density raster layer.

tools.name: TIN Interpolation
tools.description:
Generates a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN) interpolation of a
point vector layer.
With the TIN method you can create a surface formed by triangles of
nearest neighbor points.
To do this, circumcircles around selected sample points are created
and their intersections are connected to a network of non overlapping
and as compact as possible triangles.
The resulting surfaces are not smooth.
The algorithm creates both the raster layer of the interpolated values
and the vector line layer with the triangulation boundaries.

INTERPOLATION_DATA.name: INTERPOLATION_DATA
INTERPOLATION_DATA.description: Vector layer(s) and field(s) to use for the interpolation, coded in a string (see the ``ParameterInterpolationData`` class in :source:`InterpolationWidgets <python/plugins/processing/algs/qgis/ui/InterpolationWidgets.py>` for more details). The following GUI elements are provided to compose the interpolation data string: * **Vector layer** [vector: any] * **Interpolation attribute** [tablefield: numeric]: Attribute to use in the interpolation * **Use Z-coordinate for interpolation** [boolean]: Uses the layer's stored Z values ( For each of the added layer-field combinations, a type can be chosen: * :guilabel:`Points` * :guilabel:`Structured lines` * :guilabel:`Break lines` In the string, the layer-field elements are separated by ``'::|::'``. The sub-elements of the layer-field elements are separated by ``'::~::'``.

METHOD.name: METHOD
METHOD.description: Set the interpolation method to be used. One of: * :guilabel:`Linear` * :guilabel:`Clough-Toucher (cubic)`

EXTENT.name: EXTENT
EXTENT.description: Extent of the output raster layer. .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **extent_options** :end-before: **end_extent_options**

Increasing the number of rows or columns will decrease the cell size and increase the file size of the output raster. The values in ``Rows``, ``Columns``, ``Pixel Size X`` and ``Pixel Size Y`` will be updated simultaneously - doubling the number of rows will double the number of columns, and the cell size will be halved. The extent of the output raster will remain the same (approximately).

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT

discription:
This toolbox provides a concise yet practical set of utilities focused on the **packaging, information extraction, and attribute export** of layer data within a GIS project. It is designed to enhance data management and reporting efficiency, helping users quickly convert GIS data into formats suitable for spreadsheet analysis or project documentation.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Attribute Data Export:** Use the **Export to spreadsheet** tool to export the attribute table data of one or more vector layers into a spreadsheet file (e.g., Excel), supporting appending as new sheets for easy external statistical analysis and reporting.
- **Layer Information Extraction:**
    - **Export layer(s) information:** Creates a vector polygon layer representing the extent of the selected layer(s), attaching detailed metadata such as CRS, file path, and layer name as attributes for project documentation or layer indexing.
    - **Extract layer extent:** Quickly calculates and generates a vector rectangle layer representing the **minimum bounding box** of the entire input layer.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Project Reporting & Documentation:** Use `Export layer(s) information` to rapidly generate a summary of layer information (as a vector polygon layer), used to create a project layer list and extent map.
- **Attribute Statistical Analysis:** Export a specific layer's attribute table data via `Export to spreadsheet` for in-depth, non-spatial statistical analysis in Excel or other statistical software.
- **Data Boundary Definition:** Utilize `Extract layer extent` to quickly obtain the precise boundary extent of the workspace layer, useful for subsequent clipping or map extent setting.

**Implementation Notes:**
`Export to spreadsheet` supports handling multiple layers simultaneously, making it an efficient method for batch data export. The layer information extraction tools are powerful aids for metadata management and report generation in the GIS workflow.

**Tags:**
Layer Management, Attribute Export, Spreadsheet, Extent Extraction, Metadata, Bounding Box

discription:
This toolbox focuses on the creation, analysis, and data extraction of the **Mesh data model**, particularly for handling **unstructured meshes** (such as Finite Element or hydrological model outputs). It provides a bridge for users to convert complex mesh data into standard vector and raster formats, enabling traditional GIS analysis, cartography, and visualization.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Mesh Model Creation:** Use the **TIN mesh creation** tool to convert vector layers into a **Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN) mesh layer** via Delaunay triangulation.
- **Mesh Data Vectorization:** Offers a comprehensive set of export tools that convert the mesh's geometric elements (**vertices, edges, faces**) and their associated dataset values into standard vector **point, line, and polygon** layers.
- **Mesh Data Rasterization & Extraction:** Supports **Rasterize mesh dataset** to convert mesh scalar data into a traditional **raster layer**. Features **Export contours** to create vector **contour line layers** from scalar mesh data. Allows extraction of **cross section values** along vector lines and **time series values** from points for in-depth temporal or depth analysis.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Model Result Visualization:** Convert unstructured mesh data outputs from hydrodynamic or climate models into raster layers via **Rasterize mesh dataset** or contour lines via **Export contours** for standard map production.
- **Model Result Verification:** Use **Export mesh faces/vertices** to convert mesh cells and nodes into vector features, then use GIS attribute queries and spatial analysis to meticulously check and validate model calculation results.
- **Data Structure Conversion:** Use **TIN mesh creation** to generate a TIN mesh from elevation points, serving as input for advanced hydrological analysis.

**Implementation Notes:**
Mesh data models (e.g., Unstructured Grid) are often used in complex scientific computations. This toolbox is key to integrating their results into the GIS platform for secondary analysis. Data export tools attach the mesh's dataset values (e.g., flow velocity, temperature) as attributes to the new vector layers.

**Tags:**
Mesh, TIN, Rasterization, Vectorization, Cross Section, Contours, Time Series, Unstructured Grid

discription:
This toolbox is a core extension of the QGIS **Graphical Processing Modeler**, providing a set of tools for control, logical decision-making, data flow management, and auxiliary operations. It goes beyond mere geoprocessing functions, enabling users to create complex GIS workflows that are **automated, dynamic, and feature conditional branching logic**.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Workflow Control & Logic:** Use **Conditional branch** to implement conditional control over model execution; trigger termination or log information upon meeting specific criteria with **Raise exception** and **Raise warning/message** for robust error handling.
- **Variable & Expression Management:** Offers the **Calculate expression** tool to compute and store expression results, preventing redundant calculations; and can set project-level variables via **Set project variable** or perform **String concatenation** for dynamic generation of filenames or parameters.
- **Data Flow & Environment Setup:** Supports filtering and directing incoming features using **Feature filter** and **Filter layers by type**; can execute environment setup and data management operations like **Create directory** and **Rename layer**.
- **Result & Log Management:** Provides **Load layer into project** to add intermediate or final layers to the current project, and can **Save log to file** to record the model's complete execution log.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Smart Automation Model:** Create a model that first uses `Conditional branch` to check if the input data is a vector; if so, proceed with vector analysis, otherwise stop and report an error using `Raise exception`.
- **Dynamic Naming & Reporting:** At the start of the model, generate a timestamp with `Calculate expression`, then use `String concatenation` to append it to the layer name, ensuring unique output filenames. Finally, use `Save log to file` to save the execution log to the new directory.
- **Data Preparation & Filtering:** Use `Feature filter` to pass only records with a feature ID greater than 1000 to the next analysis step.

**Implementation Notes:**
This toolbox is essential for automating complex workflows. Most of its tools are only meaningful within the Modeler, used to control data flow and logic. `Calculate expression` and `Conditional branch` allow users to introduce Python script logic into the graphical model.

**Tags:**
Modeler, Automation, Workflow, Logic Control, Variable, SQL, Error Handling, Log

and use it multiple times within the model, if the timestamp

discription:
This toolbox specializes in pathfinding and accessibility analysis using **topological network models** (such as roads, pipelines, or rivers). It provides users with a set of key tools for calculating **optimal paths** (shortest or fastest) and **service areas** (by distance or time cost), making it essential for fields like transportation planning, logistics, emergency response, and infrastructure assessment.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Shortest Path Calculation:** Offers the **Shortest path** tool series, supporting the calculation of optimal routes for **point-to-point**, **multi-point-to-single-point** (layer to point), or **single-point-to-multi-point** (point to layer) scenarios. Users can optimize for either the **shortest distance** or the **fastest time** based on network costs.
- **Service Area Accessibility Analysis:** Utilizes the **Service area** tool series to calculate all reachable edges or parts of edges within the network. This determines all areas accessible from a given starting point (point layer or single point) within a **specified cost** (distance or time), used to evaluate facility coverage and accessibility.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Logistics Planning:** Use `Shortest path (point to point)` to calculate the shortest route from a distribution center to a customer, and use `Shortest path (point to layer)` to optimize the total route for a delivery person traveling from the warehouse to multiple drop-off points.
- **Emergency Response Assessment:** Use `Service area` to analyze the road network coverage accessible from a fire station or hospital within a 5-minute travel time (time cost), evaluating the emergency service response capacity.
- **Infrastructure Impact Assessment:** In a utility network, use `Service area` to calculate all downstream pipe segments that a single failure point could impact within a given maintenance distance.

**Implementation Notes:**
Prior to network analysis, the input line layer must undergo **topological checks** to ensure correct connectivity. Both shortest path and service area analysis depend on the **cost attribute** of the network edges (e.g., distance, travel time), which is typically stored in the line layer's attribute table.

**Tags:**
Network Analysis, Shortest Path, Accessibility, Service Area, Topology, Route Planning, Logistics

cost greater than a given value (the cost can be distance or time).

discription:
This toolbox provides a comprehensive set of non-spatial statistical visualization tools, focusing on **rapidly generating standard statistical charts based on layer attributes and raster values**. It enables users to perform data exploration, distribution analysis, and visualization of variable relationships directly within the GIS environment, serving as a critical aid for data quality checks and report generation.

**Core Capabilities - Revised:**

- **Distribution & Frequency Analysis:** Supports generating **Histograms** for numerical attribute fields of **vector layers** and values of **raster layers**, used to analyze data frequency distribution and skewness.
- **Central Tendency & Dispersion:** Offers **Box plots** and **Mean and standard deviation plots** to show the median, quartiles, outliers, mean, and standard deviation of data, categorized by a categorical field.
- **Variable Relationship & Comparison:** Supports generating **Bar plots** for categorical data comparison; provides **Scatter plots** and **3D Scatter plots** to visualize the relationship and correlation between two or three numerical variables.
- **Specialized Visualization:** Includes the **Polar plot** tool for representing data with periodic or directional characteristics.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Data Quality Check:** Use **Vector layer histogram** on an imported attribute field to check if the data distribution meets expectations, quickly identifying outliers or coding errors.
- **Categorical Comparison:** Use a **Box plot** to compare the differences and variability in mean building density (numerical field) among different land-use types (categorical field).
- **Report Illustration Generation:** Rapidly generate a **Bar plot** or **Scatter plot** based on analysis results to serve as statistical chart illustrations within a map analysis report.

**Implementation Notes:**
The charts generated by this toolbox are based on the layer's **attribute data** or **raster values**, making them non-spatial statistics. All plotting tools require input attribute fields to be numerical (except for categorical plots). These plots can be used directly for data exploration or exported as image files for reports.

**Tags:**
Plots, Histogram, Scatter Plot, Box Plot, Polar Plot, Data Visualization, Statistical Analysis

discription:
This toolbox is a core set of utilities based on the **PDAL (Point Data Abstraction Library)** engine, specializing in **format optimization and model conversion** of point cloud data (e.g., LiDAR). It provides users with the critical capability to integrate complex 3D point cloud data into traditional GIS raster and vector environments.

**Core Capabilities - Revised (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Format & Model Conversion:** Supports conversion between point cloud file formats and **compression (LAZ)**; allows export of point cloud data to standard **3D vector point layers** (GeoPackage).
- **Point Cloud to Rasterization:** Provides two methods for converting point clouds to 2D rasters: **fast rasterization** based on point attribute statistics; or **high-accuracy rasterization** based on **Triangulation (TIN)** interpolation (used for DEM generation).

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **High-Accuracy DEM Creation:** Generate a high-precision Digital Elevation Model (DEM) from classified ground points using **TIN Interpolation Rasterization**.
- **Data Archiving & Interoperability:** Convert large LAS files into the **compressed LAZ format** for storage optimization, or convert point cloud nodes to searchable GIS point features via **Export to vector**.

**Implementation Notes:**
This toolbox relies on PDAL, ensuring high efficiency in point cloud operations. Rasterization is the critical step for integrating point clouds with traditional GIS analysis. Using triangulation for rasterization provides higher surface accuracy.

**Tags:**
Point Cloud, LiDAR, PDAL, Rasterization, Vectorization, Format Conversion, DEM, LAZ

This toolbox is a core management suite built on the **PDAL** engine, specializing in **preprocessing, organization optimization, and spatial reference management** for large-scale point cloud data. It provides users with an efficient environment for organizing, thinning, clipping, and coordinating correcting LiDAR and photogrammetry data.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**
- **Data Structure Optimization:** Create **COPC** indexes or **Virtual Point Clouds (VPC)**, supporting **merging** and **tiling** for high-performance rendering and data access.
- **Geometry & Density Control:** Extract subsets via **polygonal clipping (Clip)**; and **thin (Thin)** the point cloud using **skipping points or sampling radius** methods to optimize performance.
- **Spatial Reference & Metadata:** Supports **Assign projection** and **Reproject** of point cloud data for alignment assurance; and provides an **Information** tool for quick metadata retrieval.

**Typical Scenarios:**
Use **Merge/COPC** to optimize the data source, then use **Clip** to extract the AOI, and finally **Thin** the data to accelerate subsequent analysis.

discription:
This toolbox is a concise, PDAL-based utility set specializing in **extracting spatial boundaries, calculating density, and subset filtering** from point cloud data. It empowers users to transform non-geometric information within point clouds into standard GIS analysis features.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**
- **Point Cloud Subset Filtering:** Use the **Filter** tool to precisely extract desired point subsets based on **PDAL expressions** (e.g., by classification code) or a **cropping rectangle**.
- **Information Extraction:** Provides the **Density** tool to calculate and output point cloud density as a **raster layer** for quality checking and hotspot analysis; uses the **Boundary** tool to extract the point cloud dataset's **precise outer polygon boundary**.

**Typical Scenarios:**
Use **Filter** to extract only ground or vegetation points, then use **Density** to check the uniformity of their distribution; or directly use **Boundary** to obtain the complex polygonal extent of the point cloud acquisition area.

**Tags:**
Point Cloud, PDAL, Filter, Density, Boundary, Extraction, Rasterization

discription:
This is a comprehensive native toolset focused on **raster algebra, statistical analysis, data reclassification, and complex spatial relationship assessment**. It provides users with the ability to perform advanced mathematical, logical, and statistical processing on single or multi-layer raster data at the pixel level, making it a core tool for multi-criteria evaluation, time-series analysis, and remote sensing data processing.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**

- **Raster Algebra:** Centered around the **Raster calculator** (including virtual), supported by **Boolean logic (AND/OR)** for threshold-based layer combination.
- **Multi-Layer Stack Analysis:** Offers **Cell statistics** (e.g., Mean, Count, Variance) and **Frequency/Percentile** toolsets for vertical statistical analysis of multiple raster layers at the same cell location.
- **Data Reclassification & Adjustment:** Supports reclassification **by fixed table or layer**; enables **Rescale** and **Round** operations to adjust raster value range and precision.
- **Statistical & Extraction Tools:** Includes **Zonal statistics/histogram**, **raster value sampling**, **surface volume** calculation, and **unique value reporting**.
- **Fuzzy Set Theory:** Provides various **Fuzzify raster** functions to convert deterministic rasters into fuzzy membership layers for fuzzy logic assessment.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Multi-Criteria Suitability Analysis:** Use the **Fuzzify** tools to convert multiple factors (e.g., slope, distance) into 0-1 membership layers, then use the **Raster calculator** for weighted overlay.
- **Time-Series Trend Analysis:** Use **Cell statistics** (e.g., Mean, Std Dev) to analyze pixel-wise change trends across a stack of multi-year remote sensing images; use **Highest/Lowest position** to determine the year of extreme values.
- **Land Use Assessment:** Use **Zonal statistics** or **Zonal histogram** to calculate the average elevation or the proportion of different land cover types within defined administrative zones (vector regions).

**Implementation Notes:**
Operations in this toolbox act on pixel values, requiring all stack analysis tools to have precise cell alignment between rasters. The `Raster calculator` is the most flexible tool but requires familiarity with its expression syntax. Fuzzification is commonly used for uncertainty modeling.

**Tags:**
Raster Algebra, Cell Statistics, Reclassify, Zonal Statistics, Fuzzy Logic, Frequency, Raster Calculator

tools.name: Cell stack percent rank from value
tools.description:
Calculates the cell-wise percentrank value of a stack of rasters based on
a single input value and writes them to an output raster.
At each cell location, the specified value is ranked among the respective values
in the stack of all overlaid and sorted cell values from the input rasters.
For values outside of the stack value distribution, the algorithm returns NoData
because the value cannot be ranked among the cell values.
There are two methods for percentile calculation:
* Inclusive linear interpolation (PERCENTRANK.INC)
* Exclusive linear interpolation (PERCENTRANK.EXC)
The linear interpolation methods return the unique percent rank for different values.
Both interpolation methods follow their counterpart methods implemented
by `LibreOffice <https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/scalc/01/04060184.html?DbPAR=CALC#bm_id3148807>`_
or Microsoft Excel.
The output raster's extent and resolution is defined by a reference raster.
Input raster layers that do not match the cell size of the reference
raster layer will be resampled using nearest neighbor resampling.
NoData values in any of the input layers will result in a NoData cell output
if the "Ignore NoData values" parameter is not set.
The output raster data type will always be ``Float32``.
  Percent ranking Value = 1. ``NoData`` cells (grey) are ignored.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgiscellstackpercentile`, :ref:`qgiscellstackpercentrankfromrasterlayer`

tools.name: Cell statistics
tools.description:
Computes per-cell statistics based on input raster layers
and for each cell writes the resulting statistics to an output raster. At each
cell location, the output value is defined as a function of all overlaid
cell values of the input rasters.
By default, a NoData cell in ANY of the input layers will result in a
NoData cell in the output raster.
If the :guilabel:`Ignore NoData values` option is checked,
then NoData inputs will be ignored in the statistic calculation. This
may result in NoData output for locations where all cells are NoData.
The :guilabel:`Reference layer` parameter specifies an existing raster layer to
use as a reference when creating the output raster.
The output raster will have the same extent, CRS, and pixel dimensions
as this layer.
**Calculation details:**
Input raster layers that do not match the cell size of the reference
raster layer will be resampled using ``nearest neighbor resampling``.
The output raster data type will be set to the most complex
data type present in the input datasets except when using the
functions ``Mean``, ``Standard deviation`` and ``Variance`` (data type is always
``Float32`` or ``Float64`` depending on input float type) or ``Count``
and ``Variety`` (data type is always ``Int32``).
- ``Count``: The count statistic will always result in the number of cells
  without NoData values at the current cell location.
- ``Median``: If the number of input layers is even, the median will be
  calculated as the arithmetic mean of the two middle values of the ordered cell input values.
- ``Minority/Majority``: If no unique minority or majority could be found,
  the result is NoData, except all input cell values are equal.
  Example with all the statistic functions. ``NoData`` cells (grey) are taken into account.

tools.name: Raster boolean AND
tools.description:
Calculates the boolean ``AND`` for a set of input rasters.
If all of the input rasters have a non-zero value for a pixel, that
pixel will be set to ``1`` in the output raster.
If any of the input rasters have ``0`` values for the pixel it will
be set to ``0`` in the output raster.
The reference layer parameter specifies an existing raster layer to
use as a reference when creating the output raster.
The output raster will have the same extent, CRS, and pixel dimensions
as this layer.
By default, a NoData pixel in ANY of the input layers will result in a
NoData pixel in the output raster.
If the :guilabel:`Treat NoData values as false` option is checked,
then NoData inputs will be treated the same as a ``0`` input value.

Performs algebraic operations using raster layers and generates in-memory result.
The resulting layer will have its values computed according to an expression.
The expression can contain numerical values, operators and references
to any of the layers in the current project.
A virtual raster layer is a raster layer defined by its URI and whose pixels are calculated on-the-fly.
It's not a new file on disk; the virtual layer is still connected to the rasters used in the calculation
meaning that deleting or moving these rasters would break it.

Alternatively, a negative number of decimal places may be used to round values
to powers of a base n. For example, with a Base value n of 10 and Decimal places

discription:
This toolbox specializes in **generating blank or randomly filled raster layers with specified extent, resolution, and data type** on demand. It is a core toolset for creating models, performing Monte Carlo simulations, random sampling, and generating constant-value raster masks.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**

- **Create Constant Raster:** Use the **Create constant raster layer** tool to generate a raster layer where all cell values within the specified extent and resolution are filled with a **fixed constant value** (often used for creating masks or uniform background layers).
- **Generate Random Raster:** Offers the **Create random raster layer** series of tools, supporting the generation of raster layers filled with random values that follow **various statistical distributions** (e.g., Normal, Uniform, Exponential, Binomial, Poisson), used for simulation and testing.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Model Input Template:** Quickly create a **constant raster** with the exact extent and resolution of the analysis area, serving as an initial input or template for other complex raster algebra operations.
- **Spatial Simulation & Sampling:** Use **Create random raster layer (normal distribution)** to generate a random (noise) raster layer with a specific mean and standard deviation for Monte Carlo simulations or random sampling.

**Implementation Notes:**
All generated rasters require the user to provide explicit **extent and cell size**. Random rasters are generated based on statistical distribution principles, forming the foundation for uncertainty analysis and spatial statistical modeling.

**Tags:**
Raster Creation, Random Raster, Constant Raster, Statistical Distribution, Monte Carlo, Template Generation

discription:
This toolbox specializes in extracting and calculating various topographic attributes and morphological features from **Digital Elevation Models (DEM)**. It offers a powerful set of tools for professionals in geomorphology, hydrology, environmental science, and cartography to understand, analyze, and visualize the earth's surface relief and structure.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**

- **Fundamental Terrain Factor Extraction:** Core functions include calculating **Slope** and **Aspect** to quantify the terrain's inclination angle and compass direction.
- **Terrain Visualization:** Generate **Hillshade** and **Relief** layers to visually represent terrain undulations through optical rendering and color classification.
- **Terrain Morphology Quantification:** Calculate the **Ruggedness index** and other metrics to quantify the heterogeneity and complexity of the terrain surface.
- **Advanced Analysis & Filtering:** Supports generating **Hypsometric curves** for watershed or regional morphological analysis; includes a **slope-based DEM filter** to classify ground and non-ground cells.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Topographic Mapping & Rendering:** Create realistic and professional-looking base maps by overlaying **Hillshade** and **Relief** onto the DEM.
- **Hydrological & Geological Analysis:** Use **Slope** and **Aspect** results to analyze surface runoff trends and potential landslide risks; use **Ruggedness index** to assess terrain complexity's influence on species distribution.
- **DEM Preprocessing:** Use the **DTM Filter (slope-based)** to differentiate ground and non-ground features in a point cloud-derived DEM to optimize terrain model quality.

**Implementation Notes:**
All tools in this toolbox require the input raster to be **elevation data (DEM)**. `Hillshade` allows custom definition of light source azimuth and altitude. `Slope` results are typically expressed in degrees. `Hypsometric curves` output results as CSV files for further statistical analysis.

**Tags:**
DEM, Slope, Aspect, Hillshade, Geomorphology, Terrain Analysis, Ruggedness, Hypsometry

tools.name: based)
tools.description:
Can be used to filter a digital elevation model in order to classify its cells into ground and object (non-ground) cells.
The tool uses concepts as described by Vosselman (2000)
and is based on the assumption that a large height difference between two nearby cells is unlikely to be caused by a steep slope in the terrain.
The probability that the higher cell might be non-ground increases when the distance between the two cells decreases.
Therefore the filter defines a maximum height difference (``dz_max``) between two cells as a function of the distance (``d``) between the cells (``dz_max( d ) = d``).
A cell is classified as terrain if there is no cell within the kernel radius
to which the height difference is larger than the allowed maximum height difference at the distance between these two cells.
The approximate terrain slope (``s``) parameter is used to modify the filter function
to match the overall slope in the study area (``dz_max( d ) = d * s``).
A 5 % confidence interval (``ci = 1.65 * sqrt( 2 * stddev )``) may be used to modify the filter function even further
by either relaxing (``dz_max( d ) = d * s + ci``) or amplifying (``dz_max( d ) = d * s - ci``) the filter criterium.
*References: Vosselman, G. (2000): Slope based filtering of laser altimetry data. IAPRS, Vol. XXXIII, Part B3, Amsterdam, The Netherlands, 935-942*
.. seealso:: This tool is a port of the SAGA `DTM Filter (slope-based) <https://saga-gis.sourceforge.io/saga_tool_doc/9.1.1/grid_filter_7.html>`_

TERRAIN_SLOPE.description: The approximate terrain slope in ``%``. The terrain slope must be adjusted to account for the ratio of height units vs raster pixel dimensions. Used to relax the filter criterium in steeper terrain.

FILTER_MODIFICATION.name: FILTER_MODIFICATION
FILTER_MODIFICATION.description: Choose whether to apply the filter kernel without modification or to use a confidence interval to relax or amplify the height criterium. * 0 - None * 1 - Relax filter * 2 - Amplify

STANDARD_DEVIATION.name: STANDARD_DEVIATION
STANDARD_DEVIATION.description: The standard deviation used to calculate a 5% confidence interval applied to the height threshold.

discription:
This toolbox is a collection of native utilities focused on **spatial calibration, data cleaning, and Web map tile generation** for raster data. It provides key tools for solving multi-source raster data interoperability issues, filling missing values, and quickly publishing project maps in online tile formats.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**

- **Data Calibration & Alignment:** Offers the **Align rasters** tool to resample and reproject multiple raster layers to the same **cell size, extent, and CRS**, ensuring precise alignment for raster algebra operations (a separate version exists for the Modeler).
- **Data Cleaning & Creation:** Use **Fill NoData cells** to replace missing values (NoData) with a specified value for data integrity repair; can convert the **current map view** or a **specific layer** into a new raster image.
- **Web Tile Publishing:** Supports fast generation of standard **XYZ Tiles** from the current QGIS project map content, with direct export to either a **directory structure** or a **single MBTiles file** for Web map deployment.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Multi-Raster Preprocessing:** Before performing complex raster algebra, use `Align rasters` to unify all input rasters to the same spatial reference and resolution.
- **Web Map Quick Deployment:** Use `Generate XYZ tiles (MBTiles)` to quickly package a base map or analysis result into a single `.mbtiles` file for mobile or Web GIS use.
- **Data Integrity Repair:** Use `Fill NoData cells` to replace NoData areas in satellite imagery or DEMs caused by sensor failure with a specific value, making them recognizable by subsequent analysis tools.

**Tags:**
Raster Alignment, NoData Fill, Web Tiles, XYZ Tiles, MBTiles, Resampling, Rasterization
