discription:
This toolbox is a powerful native utility set focused on **spatial relationships, distance, clustering, morphology, and statistical analysis** of vector data. It provides users with core tools for executing **spatial clustering, proximity assessment, overlay analysis**, and various **attribute statistics**, which are key to solving complex geospatial analysis problems.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**

- **Proximity & Distance Analysis:** Calculates the **shortest line between features** and **distance matrix**; uses **Distance to nearest hub** and **Join by lines (hub lines)** to create connection lines from features to the nearest center for logistics and radiation analysis.
- **Spatial Clustering & Morphology:** Offers **DBSCAN** and **K-means** clustering algorithms and **Nearest neighbour analysis** to identify spatial aggregation patterns and distribution types of point features; can compute the **mean coordinates** (center of mass).
- **Overlay & Counting Analysis:** Supports **Count points in polygon** and **Sum line lengths**; performs **Overlap analysis** to calculate the area and percentage cover of feature overlaps.
- **Attribute & Terrain Statistics:** Extracts **basic statistics** and **unique value lists** for fields; supports **statistics by categories**; and can calculate the **total climb and descent (Climb along line)** for 3D line features for path analysis.

**Typical Scenarios:**

- **Logistics & Emergency Planning:** Use **Distance to nearest hub** to determine the nearest distribution center for each customer point, and create hub-and-spoke diagrams using **Join by lines**.
- **Spatial Clustering Analysis:** Utilize **DBSCAN clustering** to identify hotspots of crime incidents or epidemic data, and verify the non-randomness of their spatial distribution with **Nearest neighbour analysis**.
- **Land Use Assessment:** Use **Count points in polygon** or **Sum line lengths** to count the number of shops or total road length within each administrative area for regional facility assessment.

**Implementation Notes:**
This toolbox relies on vector geometry and attributes. All distance and clustering algorithms are based on 2D Cartesian coordinates (unless otherwise specified). Clustering algorithms require the user to set appropriate distance thresholds or cluster numbers based on data characteristics.

**Tags:**
Spatial Statistics, Clustering, DBSCAN, Distance Analysis, Proximity, Hub Lines, Overlay Analysis, Attribute Statistics

tools.name: Join by lines (hub lines)

Creates hub and spoke diagrams by connecting lines from points on
the Spoke layer to matching points in the Hub layer.
Determination of which hub goes with each point is based on a match
between the Hub ID field on the hub points and the Spoke ID field on
the spoke points.
If input layers are not point layers, a point on the surface of the
geometries will be taken as the connecting location.
Optionally, geodesic lines can be created, which represent the
shortest path on the surface of an ellipsoid.
When geodesic mode is used, it is possible to split the created lines
at the antimeridian (±180 degrees longitude), which can improve
rendering of the lines.
Additionally, the distance between vertices can be specified.
A smaller distance results in a denser, more accurate line.
  Join points based on a common field / attribute

features.

how your data are distributed (clustered, randomly or distributed).

* Nearest neighbour index

discription:
This toolbox specializes in creating new vector geometries (point, line, polygon) **from scratch, based on existing data, or derived from models**. It provides a core set of tools for generating various **regular/random samples**, **geometric copies**, and performing **raster/table-to-vector** model conversions.

**Core Capabilities (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Geometry Generation & Duplication:** Supports **creating regular grids (Create grid)**; allows features to be **translated** or **offset** to generate **array copies**; and converts ordered points into **path lines (Points to path)**.
- **Sampling & Random Points:** Offers the **Random points** tool series to generate **random points** within a given extent, layer bounds, polygons, or lines; also supports **regular point** generation and **pixel centroid point** generation along lines.
- **Data Import & Model Conversion:** Core functions include importing XY(Z) coordinate points from a **table** (CSV/Excel); importing locations from **geotagged photos**; and converting **raster pixels** into **point** or **polygon** vector features.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Sampling & Survey:** Use **Random points in polygons** to create random survey sample points within a study area, and use **Import geotagged photos** to import field photo locations.
- **Grid Generation:** Use **Create grid** to generate hexagonal or rectangular grids to serve as **uniform analysis units** for spatial statistics (e.g., crime grid analysis).
- **Model Conversion:** Use **Raster pixels to points/polygons** to convert classified raster results (e.g., land use maps) into vector features for overlay analysis.

**Tags:**
Vector Creation, Random Points, Regular Grid, Raster to Vector, Sampling, Geometry Copy, GPS, Table Import

tools.name: Array of offset (parallel) lines

Creates copies of line features in a layer, by creating multiple
offset versions of each feature.
Each new version is incrementally offset by a specified distance.
Positive distance will offset lines to the left, and negative
distances will offset them to the right.
   In blue the source layer, in red the offset one
of line features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisoffsetline`, :ref:`qgisarraytranslatedfeatures`

MITER_LIMIT.description: Sets the maximum distance from the offset geometry to use when creating a mitered join as a factor of the offset distance (only applicable for miter join styles). Minimum: 1.0 A 10m buffer with a limit of 2 and a 10m buffer with a limit of 1

tools.name: Random points along line
tools.description:
Creates a new point layer, with points placed on the lines of another
layer.
For each line in the input layer, a given number of points is added
to the resulting layer.
The procedure for adding a point is to:
1. randomly select a line feature from the input layer
2. if the feature is multi-part, randomly select a part of it
3. randomly select a segment of that line
4. randomly select a position on that segment.
The procedure means that curved parts of the lines (with relatively
short segments) will get more points than straight parts (with
relatively long segments), as demonstrated in the illustration below,
where the output of the *Random points along lines* algorithm can be
compared with the output of the *Random points on lines* algorithm
(that produces points with an, on average, even distribution along
the lines).
   Example algorithm output. Left: *Random points along line*, right:
   *Random points on lines*
A minimum distance can be specified, to avoid points being too close
to each other.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisrandompointsonlines`

layer, the given number of points is added to the result layer.
Per feature and global minimum distances can be specified in order to
avoid points being too close in the output point layer.
If a minimum distance is specified, it may not be possible to generate
the specified number of points for each feature.
The total number of generated points and missed points are available
as output from the algorithm.
The illustration below shows the effect of per feature and global
minimum distances and zero/non-zero minimum distances (generated with
the same seed, so at least the first point generated will be the
same).
   Ten points per polygon feature, *left*: min. distances = 0,
   *middle*: min.distances = 1, *right*: min. distance = 1,
   global min. distance = 0
The maximum number of tries per point can be specified.
This is only relevant for non-zero minimum distance.
A seed for the random number generator can be provided, making it
possible to get identical random number sequences for different runs
of the algorithm.
The attributes of the polygon feature on which a point was generated
can be included (:guilabel:`Include polygon attributes`).
If you want approximately the same point density for all the
features, you can data-define the number of points using the area of
the polygon feature geometry.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisrandompointsinsidepolygons`

discription:
This toolbox is the most extensive and core vector utility collection in QGIS, focusing on **spatial reference, attribute joining, data organization, cleaning, and I/O (Input/Output)** of vector data. It provides key tools for handling multi-source data, correcting errors, optimizing performance, and performing complex data integration.

**Core Capabilities (Extreme Concise):**

- **Spatial Reference & Transformation:** Performs **Reproject layer** for geometry transformation; **Assign/Define projection** to correct or set the CRS; and supports **Find projection** to assist in identifying unknown CRSs.
- **Attribute & Spatial Joins:** Supports joining attributes in three ways: **by field value**, **by location** (including **with summary statistics**), and **by nearest neighbour**; allows for data restructuring using **Flatten relationship** and **Split features by character**.
- **Data Organization & Optimization:** Supports **Merge vector layers** and **Split vector layer**; used to delete **duplicate geometries/attributes**; can create **spatial/attribute indexes** to optimize query performance, and performs **Detect dataset changes** for version comparison.
- **I/O & Utilities:** Provides **Execute SQL** for advanced queries; enables **Batch Nominatim geocoder** for bulk address conversion; supports data transfer and management via **Export to DXF**, **Save to file**, and **Create/Convert spatial bookmarks**.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Data Integration:** Merge layers from different sources using **Merge vector layers**, then use **Join attributes by location** to aggregate statistical data by region.
- **Data Cleaning:** Clean duplicate records with **Delete duplicates by attribute** and repair damaged files with **Repair Shapefile**.
- **Performance Optimization:** Use **Create spatial/attribute index** on large layers to optimize query and rendering speed.
- **Address Conversion:** Use **Batch Nominatim geocoder** to convert address fields in the attribute table into precise point locations on the map.

**Tags:**
Data Management, Attribute Join, Spatial Join, Projection, SQL, Performance Optimization, Encoding, Merge, Split, Attribute Table

tools.name: Execute SQL
tools.description:
Runs a simple or complex query based only on SELECT with ``SQL`` syntax 
on the source layer.
Input datasources are identified with ``input1``, ``input2``... ``inputN`` and
a simple query will look like ``SELECT * FROM input1``.
Beside a simple query, you can add expressions or variables within the 
``SQL query`` parameter itself. This is particulary useful if this algorithm is
executed within a Processing model and you want to use a model input as a
parameter of the query. An example of a query will then be ``SELECT * FROM 
[% @table %]`` where ``@table`` is the variable that identifies the model input.
The result of the query will be added as a new layer.

the first input layer.

discription:
This toolbox is a vast collection of native tools focused on the **precise creation, modification, and repair of vector feature geometry, topology, and spatial dimensions**. It provides a full range of solutions from basic buffering to advanced affine transformations, and from geometry validation to 3D attribute setting.

**Core Capabilities (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Geometry Repair & Validation:** Executes **Check validity** and **Fix geometries** for topological error handling; enables **deleting holes**, **removing duplicate vertices**, or **null geometries** to ensure data quality.
- **Distance & Buffering:** Creates standard **Buffer**, **Single sided buffer**, **Multi-ring**, and **Variable width buffers**; supports **Minimum bounding geometry** (circle, box, convex hull) and **Voronoi/Delaunay** structures.
- **Morphology & Dimension:** Supports **Simplify/Smooth**, **Densify**, **Subdivide**, and **Orthogonalize**; enables **Aggregate/Collect** or **Multipart to singleparts**; allows **Affine transform**, **Translate**, and **Rotate** for geometric manipulation.
- **3D/M Value & Vertex Ops:** **Drape (set Z/M value from raster)** extracts elevation/M values from rasters onto geometries; supports **extracting vertices** and **filtering Z/M values**; calculates **geometry attributes (Add geometry attributes)**.
- **Topological Boundary & Conversion:** **Lines to Polygons/Polygons to lines** converts geometry type; extracts **Boundary**, **Centroids**, and **Pole of inaccessibility**.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Data Preparation:** Use **Simplify/Smooth** to refine feature outlines; use **Check validity** to find topological errors and **Fix geometries** to repair them.
- **3D Modeling:** Use **Drape (set Z value from raster)** to set elevation for road lines, then use **Buffer** to create 3D buffers.
- **Advanced Structures:** Use **Voronoi polygons** for proximity partitioning; use **Pole of inaccessibility** to determine the most distant internal point from a boundary.

**Tags:**
Geometry Processing, Buffer, Simplify, Repair, Topology, 3D, Voronoi, Aggregate, Vertex, Affine Transform

tools.name: Add geometry attributes

Computes geometric properties of the features in a vector layer and
includes them in the output layer.
It generates a new vector layer with the same content as the input one,
but with additional attributes, containing geometric measurements
based on a selected CRS.
The attributes added to the table depend on the geometry type and
dimension of the input layer:
* for **point** layers: X (``xcoord``), Y (``ycoord``), Z (``zcoord``)
  coordinates and/or M value (``mvalue``)
* for **line** layers: ``length`` and, for the LineString and
  CompoundCurve geometry types, the feature ``sinuosity`` and straight
  distance (``straightdis``)
* for **polygon** layers: ``perimeter`` and ``area``
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Vector --> Geometry Tools`

tools.name: Aggregate
tools.description:
Takes a vector or table layer and creates a new layer by aggregating
features based on a ``group by`` expression.
Features for which ``group by`` expression returns the same value are
grouped together.
It is possible to group all source features together using constant
value in ``group by`` parameter, example: NULL.
It is also possible to group features by multiple fields using Array
function, example: Array("Field1", "Field2").
Geometries (if present) are combined into one multipart geometry for
each group.
Output attributes are computed depending on each given aggregate
definition.
This algorithm allows to use the default
:ref:`aggregates functions <aggregates_function>` of the QGIS Expression engine.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgiscollect`, :ref:`qgisdissolve`

In the GUI, you can edit these fields and their definitions, and you can also: * Click the button to add a new field. * Click to delete the selected field. * Use and to change order of the fields. * Click to reset to the default (the fields of the input layer). For each of the fields you'd like to retrieve information from, you need to define the following: ``Input expression`` [expression] (``input``) Field or expression from the input layer. ``Aggregate function`` [enumeration] (``aggregate``) :ref:`Function <aggregates_function>` to use on the input expression to return the aggregated value. numeric data type) ``Delimiter`` [string] (``delimiter``) Text string to separate aggregated values, for example in case of concatenation. ``Output field name`` [string] (``name``) Name of the aggregated field in the output layer. By default input field name is kept. ``Type`` [enumeration] (``type``) Data type of the output field. One of: * 1 --- Boolean * 2 --- Integer * 4 --- Integer64 * 6 --- Double * 10 --- String * 14 --- Date * 16 --- DateTime ``Length`` [number] (``length``) Length of the output field. ``Precision`` [number] (``precision``) Precision of the output field.

OUTPUT.description: Specify the output (bounding box) layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Bounds
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Bounding boxes of input layer. Other than the input attributes, the output layer also contains following fields: ``width``, ``height``, ``area`` and ``perimeter`` of the generated polygon.

tools.name: Buffer
tools.description:
Computes a buffer area for all the features in an input layer, using
a fixed or data defined distance.
It is possible to use a negative distance for polygon input layers.
In this case the buffer will result in a smaller polygon (setback).
   Buffer (in yellow) of points, line, polygon with positive buffer, 
   and polygon with negative buffer 
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>` 
of polygon features
   :ref:`qgismultiringconstantbuffer`, :ref:`qgisbufferbym`

DISTANCE.name: DISTANCE
DISTANCE.description: Buffer distance (from the boundary of each feature). You can use the Data Defined button on the right to choose a field from which the radius will be calculated. This way you can have different radius for each feature (see :ref:`qgisvariabledistancebuffer`).

SEGMENTS.name: SEGMENTS
SEGMENTS.description: Controls the number of line segments to use to approximate a quarter circle when creating rounded offsets.

END_CAP_STYLE.name: END_CAP_STYLE
END_CAP_STYLE.description: Controls how line endings are handled in the buffer. One of: * 0 --- Round * 1 --- Flat * 2 --- Square Round, flat and square cap styles

JOIN_STYLE.name: JOIN_STYLE
JOIN_STYLE.description: Specifies whether round, miter or beveled joins should be used when offsetting corners in a line. Options are: * 0 --- Round * 1 --- Miter * 2 --- Bevel Round, miter, and bevel join styles

MITER_LIMIT.name: MITER_LIMIT
MITER_LIMIT.description: Sets the maximum distance from the offset geometry to use when creating a mitered join as a factor of the offset distance (only applicable for miter join styles). Minimum: 1.0 A 10m buffer with a limit of 2 and a 10m buffer with a limit of 1

DISSOLVE.name: DISSOLVE
DISSOLVE.description: Dissolve the final buffer. If ``True`` (checked), overlapping buffers will be dissolved (combined) into a single multipart feature. Standard (three single part features - left), dissolved (1 multipart feature with 2 parts - right)

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output (buffer) layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

SEPARATE_DISJOINT.name: SEPARATE_DISJOINT
SEPARATE_DISJOINT.description: If ``True`` (checked) and dissolved is checked, features that do not overlap or touch will be exported as separate features (instead of parts of a multipart feature). Results in 2 single part features

OUTPUT.label: Buffered
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Output (buffer) polygon layer

tools.name: Centroids
tools.description:
Creates a new point layer, with points representing the centroids
of the geometries of the input layer.
The centroid is a single point representing the barycenter (of all
parts) of the feature, so it can be outside the feature borders.
But can also be a point on each part of the feature.
The attributes of the points in the output layer are the same
as for the original features.
   The red stars represent the centroids of the features of the
   input layer.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of point features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgispointonsurface`

ALL_PARTS.name: ALL_PARTS
ALL_PARTS.description: If True (checked), a centroid will be created for each part of the geometry

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output (centroid) layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Centroids
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Output point vector layer (centroids)

tools.name: Check validity
tools.description:
Performs a validity check on the geometries of a vector layer.
The geometries are classified in three groups (valid, invalid and
error) and for each group, a vector layer with its features is
generated:
* The **Valid output** layer contains only the valid features (without
  topological errors).
* The **Invalid output** layer contains all the invalid features found
  by the algorithm.
* The **Error output** layer is a point layer that points to where the
  invalid features were found.
The attribute tables of the generated layers will contain some
additional information ("message" for the **error** layer, "FID" and
"_errors" for the **invalid** layer and  only "FID" for the **valid**
layer):
The attribute table of each generated vector layer will contain some
additional information (number of errors found and types of error):
   Left: the input layer. Right: the valid layer (green), the invalid
   layer (orange)
   :ref:`geometry_checker`

METHOD.name: METHOD
METHOD.description: Method to use to check validity. Options: * 0: The one selected in digitizing settings * 1: QGIS * 2: GEOS

IGNORE_RING_SELF_INTERSECTION.name: IGNORE_RING_SELF_INTERSECTION
IGNORE_RING_SELF_INTERSECTION.description: Ignore self intersecting rings when checking for validity.

INVALID_OUTPUT.name: INVALID_OUTPUT
INVALID_OUTPUT.description: Vector layer containing copy of the invalid features of the source layer with the field ``_errors`` listing the summary of the error(s) found. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_skip** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_skip**

ERROR_OUTPUT.name: ERROR_OUTPUT
ERROR_OUTPUT.description: Point layer of the exact position of the validity problems detected with the ``message`` field describing the error(s) found. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_skip** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_skip**

ERROR_COUNT.label: Count of errors
ERROR_COUNT.name: ERROR_COUNT
ERROR_COUNT.description: The number of geometries that caused errors.

ERROR_OUTPUT.label: Error output
ERROR_OUTPUT.name: ERROR_OUTPUT
ERROR_OUTPUT.description: Point layer of the exact position of the validity problems detected with the ``message`` field describing the error(s) found.

INVALID_OUTPUT.label: Invalid output
INVALID_OUTPUT.name: INVALID_OUTPUT
INVALID_OUTPUT.description: Vector layer containing copy of the invalid features of the source layer with the field ``_errors`` listing the summary of the error(s) found.

tools.name: Collect geometries
tools.description:
Takes a vector layer and collects its geometries into new multipart
geometries.
One or more attributes can be specified to collect only geometries
belonging to the same class (having the same value for the specified
attributes), alternatively all geometries can be collected.
All output geometries will be converted to multi geometries, even
those with just a single part.
This algorithm does not dissolve overlapping geometries - they will
be collected together without modifying the shape of each geometry
part.
See the 'Promote to multipart' or 'Aggregate' algorithms for
alternative options.
   :ref:`qgisdissolve`

FIELD.name: FIELD
FIELD.description: Choose one or more attributes to collect the geometries

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Vector layer with collected geometries

tools.name: Concave hull
tools.description:
Computes the concave hull of the features from an input point layer.
    Concave hulls with different thresholds (0.3, 0.6, 0.9)
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisconvexhull`

ALPHA.name: ALPHA
ALPHA.description: Number from 0 (maximum concave hull) to 1 (convex hull).

HOLES.name: HOLES
HOLES.description: Choose whether to allow holes in the final concave hull

NO_MULTIGEOMETRY.name: NO_MULTIGEOMETRY
NO_MULTIGEOMETRY.description: Check if you want to have singlepart geometries instead of multipart ones.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Concave hull
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output vector layer

tools.name: Convert geometry type
tools.description:
Generates a new layer based on an existing one, with a different type
of geometry.
The attribute table of the output layer is the same as the one of
the input layer.
Not all conversions are possible. For instance, a line layer
can be converted to a point layer, but a point layer cannot
be converted to a line layer.
   :ref:`qgispointstopath`

TYPE.name: TYPE
TYPE.description: Geometry type to apply to the output features. One of: * 0 --- Centroids * 1 --- Nodes * 2 --- Linestrings * 3 --- Multilinestrings * 4 --- Polygons

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Converted
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Output vector layer - the type depends on the parameters

tools.name: Convert to curved geometries
tools.description:
Converts a geometry into its curved geometry equivalent.
Already curved geometries will be retained without change.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line and polygon features

DISTANCE.name: DISTANCE
DISTANCE.description: The maximum distance allowed between the original location of vertices and where they would fall on the converted curved geometries

ANGLE.name: ANGLE
ANGLE.description: Segments are considered as suitable for replacing with an arc if the points are all regularly spaced on the candidate arc. This parameter specifies the maximum angular deviation (in degrees) allowed when testing for regular point spacing. Between 0 and 45\°.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Curves
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Output vector layer with curved geometries

tools.name: Convex hull
tools.description:
Calculates the convex hull for each feature in an input layer.
See the 'Minimum bounding geometry' algorithm for a convex hull
calculation which covers the whole layer or grouped subsets of
features.
   Black lines identify the convex hull for each layer feature
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of polygon features
   :ref:`qgisconcavehull`

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Convex hull
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (convex hull) vector layer

tools.name: Create layer from extent
tools.description:
Creates a new vector layer that contains a single feature with
geometry matching the extent of the input layer.
It can be used in models to convert a literal extent (``xmin``,
``xmax``, ``ymin``, ``ymax`` format) into a layer which can be used
for other algorithms which require a layer based input.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgispointtolayer`

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Extent
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (extent) vector layer

tools.name: Create layer from point
tools.description:
Creates a new vector layer that contains a single feature with
geometry matching a point parameter.
It can be used in models to convert a point into a point layer for
algorithms which require a layer based input.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisextenttolayer`

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Input point, including CRS info (example: ``397254,6214446 [EPSG:32632]``). If the CRS is not provided, the Project CRS will be used. The point can be specified by clicking on the map canvas.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Point
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output point vector layer containing the input point.

tools.name: Create wedge buffers
tools.description:
Creates wedge shaped buffers from input points.
   Wedge buffers
The native output from this algorithm are CurvePolygon geometries,
but these may be automatically segmentized to Polygons depending
on the output format.
   :ref:`qgistaperedbuffer`

AZIMUTH.name: AZIMUTH
AZIMUTH.description: Angle (in degrees) as the middle value of the wedge

WIDTH.name: WIDTH
WIDTH.description: Width (in degrees) of the buffer. The wedge will extend to half of the angular width either side of the azimuth direction. Azimuth and width values of the wedge buffer

OUTER_RADIUS.name: OUTER_RADIUS
OUTER_RADIUS.description: The outer *size* (length) of the wedge: the size is meant from the source point to the edge of the wedge shape.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (wedge buffer) vector layer

tools.name: Delaunay triangulation
tools.description:
Creates a polygon layer with the Delaunay triangulation corresponding
to the input point layer.
   Delaunay triangulation on points
**Default menu**: :menuselection:`Vector --> Geometry Tools`

ADD_ATTRIBUTES.name: ADD_ATTRIBUTES
ADD_ATTRIBUTES.description: Specifies whether fields storing involved point features ID should be added to the output. If False, an ``id`` field is used to identify the polygons.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Delaunay triangulation
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (Delaunay triangulation) vector layer

tools.name: Delete holes
tools.description:
Takes a polygon layer and removes holes in polygons.
It creates a new vector layer in which polygons with holes have been
replaced by polygons with only their external ring.
Attributes are not modified.
An optional minimum area parameter allows removing only holes which
are smaller than a specified area threshold. Leaving this parameter at
``0.0`` results in all holes being removed.
   Before and after the cleaning
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of polygon features

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Cleaned
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (cleaned) vector layer

tools.name: Densify by count
tools.description:
Takes a polygon or line layer and generates a new one in which the
geometries have a larger number of vertices than the original one.
If the geometries have Z or M values present then these will be
linearly interpolated at the added vertices.
The number of new vertices to add to each segment is specified as an
input parameter.
   Red points show the vertices before and after the densify
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line and polygon features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisdensifygeometriesgivenaninterval`

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Input line or polygon vector layer

VERTICES.name: VERTICES
VERTICES.description: Number of vertices to add to each segment

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Densified
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (densified) vector layer

tools.name: Densify by interval
tools.description:
Takes a polygon or line layer and generates a new one in which the
geometries have a larger number of vertices than the original one.
The geometries are densified by adding regularly placed extra
vertices inside each segment so that the maximum distance between
any two vertices does not exceed the specified distance.
If the geometries have Z or M values present then these will be
linearly interpolated at the added vertices.
**Example**
Specifying a distance of 3 would cause the segment
``[0 0] -> [10 0]`` to be converted to
``[0 0] -> [2.5 0] -> [5 0] -> [7.5 0] -> [10 0]``,
since 3 extra vertices are required on the segment and spacing these
at 2.5 increments allows them to be evenly spaced over the segment.
   Densify geometry at a given interval
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line and polygon features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisdensifygeometries`

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Input line or polygon vector layer

INTERVAL.name: INTERVAL
INTERVAL.description: Maximum distance between two consecutive vertices

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Densified
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (densified) vector layer

tools.name: Dissolve
tools.description:
Takes a vector layer and combines its features into new features.
One or more attributes can be specified to dissolve features
belonging to the same class (having the same value for the specified
attributes), alternatively all features can be dissolved to a single
feature.
All output geometries will be converted to multi geometries.
In case the input is a polygon layer, common boundaries of adjacent
polygons being dissolved will get erased.
If enabled, the optional "Keep disjoint features separate" setting will
cause features and parts that do not overlap or touch to be exported as 
separate features (instead of parts of a single multipart feature).
The resulting attribute table will have the same fields as the input
layer.
The values in the output layer's fields are the ones of the first
input feature that happens to be processed.
   Dissolving a layer into a single multipart feature
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisaggregate`, :ref:`qgiscollect`

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

SEPARATE_DISJOINT.name: SEPARATE_DISJOINT
SEPARATE_DISJOINT.description: Parts of dissolved features are exported as separate features (instead of parts of a multipart feature). source (left), dissolve all (3 distinct features - right) source (left), dissolve on field (5 distinct features - right)

OUTPUT.label: Dissolved
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output vector layer with dissolved geometries

tools.name: Drape (set Z value from raster)
tools.description:
Uses values sampled from a band within a raster layer to set the Z
value for every overlapping vertex in the feature geometry.
The raster values can optionally be scaled by a preset amount.
If Z values already exist in the layer, they will be overwritten with
the new value.
If no Z values exist, the geometry will be upgraded to include the Z
dimension.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of point, line, and polygon features with Z enabled
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgissetmfromraster`, :ref:`qgissetzvalue`

BAND.name: BAND
BAND.description: The raster band to take the Z values from

NODATA.name: NODATA
NODATA.description: Value to use in case the vertex does not intersect (a valid pixel of) the raster

SCALE.name: SCALE
SCALE.description: Scaling value: the band values are multiplied by this value.

OFFSET.name: OFFSET
OFFSET.description: Offset value: it is algebraically added to the band values after applying the "Scale factor".

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer (with Z values from the raster layer). One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Updated
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output vector layer with Z values from the raster layer

tools.name: Z values
tools.description:
Removes M (measure) or Z (altitude) values from input geometries.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgissetmvalue`, :ref:`qgissetzvalue`

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Input vector layer with M or Z values

DROP_M_VALUES.name: DROP_M_VALUES
DROP_M_VALUES.description: Removes the M values from the geometries

DROP_Z_VALUES.name: DROP_Z_VALUES
DROP_Z_VALUES.description: Removes the Z values from the geometries

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Z/M Dropped
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output vector layer (identical to the input layer, except that the M and/or Z dimensions have been removed from the geometries).

tools.name: Eliminate selected polygons
tools.description:
Combines selected polygons of the input layer with certain adjacent
polygons by erasing their common boundary.
The adjacent polygon can be either the one with the largest or
smallest area or the one sharing the largest common boundary with the
polygon to be eliminated.
Eliminate is normally used to get rid of sliver polygons, i.e. tiny
polygons that are a result of polygon intersection processes where
boundaries of the inputs are similar but not identical.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisfixgeometries`

MODE.name: MODE
MODE.description: Choose the parameter to use in order to get rid of the selected polygons: * 0 --- Largest Area * 1 --- Smallest Area * 2 --- Largest Common Boundary

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Eliminated
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output polygon vector layer.

tools.name: Explode lines
tools.description:
Takes a lines layer and creates a new one in which each line layer is
replaced by a set of lines representing the segments in the original
line.
Each line in the resulting layer contains only a start and an end
point, with no intermediate vertices between them.
   The original line layer and the exploded one
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgissubdivide`, :ref:`qgislinesubstring`

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Exploded
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output line vector layer with features representing each segment of the input layer.

tools.name: Extend lines
tools.description:
Extends line geometry by a specified amount at the start and end of
the line.
Lines are extended using the bearing of the first and last segment in
the line.
   The red dashes represent the initial and final extension of the
   original layer
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgislinesubstring`

START_DISTANCE.name: START_DISTANCE
START_DISTANCE.description: Distance by which to extend the first segment of the line (starting point)

END_DISTANCE.name: END_DISTANCE
END_DISTANCE.description: Distance by which to extend the last segment of the line (ending point)

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Extended
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (extended) line vector layer.

tools.name: Extract M values
tools.description:
Extracts M values from geometries into feature attributes.
By default only the M value from the first vertex of each feature is
extracted, however the algorithm can optionally calculate statistics
on all of the geometry's M values, including sum, mean, minimum and
maximum.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisextractzvalues`, :ref:`qgissetmvalue`, :ref:`qgisdropmzvalues`

One or more of: * 0 --- First * 1 --- Last * 2 --- Count * 3 --- Sum * 4 --- Mean * 5 --- Median * 6 --- St.dev (pop) * 7 --- Minimum * 8 --- Maximum * 9 --- Range * 10 --- Minority * 11 --- Majority * 12 --- Variety * 13 --- Q1 * 14 --- Q3 * 15 --- IQR

COLUMN_PREFIX.name: COLUMN_PREFIX
COLUMN_PREFIX.description: The prefix for the output (M) column

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output vector layer (with M values)

tools.name: Extract specific vertices
tools.description:
Takes a vector layer and generates a point layer with points
representing specific vertices in the input geometries.
For instance, this algorithm can be used to extract the first or last
vertices in the geometry.
The attributes associated to each point are the same ones associated
to the feature that the vertex belongs to.
The vertex indices parameter accepts a comma separated string
specifying the indices of the vertices to extract.
The first vertex corresponds to an index of 0, the second vertex has
an index of 1, etc. Negative indices can be used to find vertices at
the end of the geometry, e.g., an index of -1 corresponds to the last
vertex, -2 corresponds to the second last vertex, etc.
Additional fields are added to the vertices indicating the specific
vertex position (e.g., 0, -1, etc), the original vertex index, the
vertex’s part and its index within the part (as well as its ring for
polygons), distance along the original geometry and bisector angle of
vertex for the original geometry.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of point features
   :ref:`qgisfilterverticesbyz`

VERTICES.name: VERTICES
VERTICES.description: Comma-separated string of the indices of the vertices to extract.

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the output vector layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types_append** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types_append**

OUTPUT.label: Vertices
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (point) vector layer containing the specified vertices from the input layer geometries.

tools.name: Extract vertices
tools.description:
Takes a vector layer and generates a point layer with points
representing the vertices in the input geometries.
The attributes associated to each point are the same ones associated
to the feature that the vertex belongs to.
Additional fields are added to the vertices indicating the vertex
index (beginning at 0), the feature’s part and its index within the
part (as well as its ring for polygons), distance along original
geometry and bisector angle of vertex for original geometry.
   Vertices extracted for line and polygon layer

of point features
   :ref:`qgisfilterverticesbym`, :ref:`qgisfilterverticesbyz`

OUTPUT.label: Vertices
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: The output (point) vector layer containing the vertices from the input layer geometries.

tools.description:
Extracts Z values from geometries into feature attributes.
By default only the Z value from the first vertex of each feature is
extracted, however the algorithm can optionally calculate statistics
on all of the geometry's Z values, including sum, mean, minimum and
maximum.
   :ref:`qgisdropmzvalues`

SUMMARIES.name: SUMMARIES
SUMMARIES.description: Statistics on the Z values of a geometry. One or more of: * 0 --- First * 1 --- Last * 2 --- Count * 3 --- Sum * 4 --- Mean * 5 --- Median * 6 --- St.dev (pop) * 7 --- Minimum * 8 --- Maximum * 9 --- Range * 10 --- Minority * 11 --- Majority * 12 --- Variety * 13 --- Q1 * 14 --- Q3 * 15 --- IQR

COLUMN_PREFIX.name: COLUMN_PREFIX

with only vertex points that have a M value greater than or equal to
the specified minimum value and/or less than or equal to the maximum
value.
If the minimum value is not specified then only the maximum value is
tested, and similarly if the maximum value is not specified then only
the minimum value is tested.

   value is <=10.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line and polygon features with M enabled
.. note:: Depending on the input geometry attributes and the filters
   used, the resultant geometries created by this algorithm may no
   longer be valid.

without losing any of the input vertices.
Already valid geometries are returned without further intervention.

.. note:: M values will be dropped from the output.
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgischeckvalidity`

One of: * 0 --- ``Linework``: combines all rings into a set of noded lines and then extracts valid polygons from that linework * 1 --- ``Structure``: first makes all rings valid and then merges shells and subtracts holes from shells to generate valid result. Assumes that holes and shells are correctly categorized. Requires QGIS version built with GEOS 3.10 or later (check :menuselection:`Help --> About` menu).

tools.name: Geodesic line split at antimeridian
tools.description:
Splits a line into multiple geodesic segments, whenever
the line crosses the antimeridian (±180 degrees longitude).
Splitting at the antimeridian helps the visual display of the lines in
some projections.
The returned geometry will always be a multi-part geometry.
Whenever line segments in the input geometry cross the antimeridian,
they will be split into two segments, with the latitude of the
breakpoint being determined using a geodesic line connecting the
points either side of this segment.
The current project ellipsoid setting will be used when calculating
this breakpoint.
If the input geometry contains M or Z values, these will be linearly
interpolated for the new vertices created at the antimeridian.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line features

For help with QGIS expression functions, see the inbuilt help available

the most distant internal point from the boundary of the surface.

2016), which is an iterative approach guaranteed to find the true pole
of inaccessibility within a specified tolerance.
A more precise tolerance (lower value) requires more iterations and
will take longer to calculate.
The distance from the calculated pole to the polygon boundary will be
stored as a new attribute in the output layer.

tools.name: Remove duplicate vertices
tools.description:
Removes duplicate vertices from features, wherever removing the
vertices does not result in a degenerate geometry.
The tolerance parameter specifies the tolerance for coordinates when
determining whether vertices are identical.
By default, Z values are not considered when detecting duplicate
vertices.
E.g. two vertices with the same X and Y coordinate but different Z
values will still be considered duplicate and one will be removed.
If the :guilabel:`Use Z Value` parameter is true, then the Z values
are also tested and vertices with the same X and Y but different Z
will be maintained.
of point, line, and polygon features
.. note:: Duplicate vertices are not tested between different parts
   of a multipart geometry, e.g. a multipoint geometry with
   overlapping points will not be changed by this method.
   :ref:`qgisextractspecificvertices`,
   :ref:`qgisdeleteduplicategeometries`

TOLERANCE.description: Vertices closer than the specified distance are considered duplicates

USE_Z_VALUE.name: USE_Z_VALUE
USE_Z_VALUE.description: If the :guilabel:`Use Z Value` parameter is true, then the Z values are also tested and vertices with the same X and Y but different Z will be maintained.

removes features whose geometries have no coordinates, i.e., geometries
that are empty.
In that case, also the null output will reflect this option, containing
both null and empty geometries.

tools.name: Smooth
tools.description:
Smooths the geometries in a line or polygon layer by
adding more **vertices and corners** to the feature geometries.
The iterations parameter dictates how many smoothing iterations will
be applied to each geometry.
A higher number of iterations results in smoother geometries with the
cost of greater number of nodes in the geometries.
    Increasing number of iterations causes smoother geometries
The offset parameter controls how "tightly" the smoothed geometries
follow the original geometries. Smaller values results in a tighter
fit, and larger values will create a looser fit.
    Blue: the input layer. Offset 0.25 gives the red line, while
    offset 0.50 gives the green line.
The maximum angle parameter can be used to prevent smoothing of nodes
with large angles.
Any node where the angle of the segments to either side is larger than
this will not be smoothed. For example, setting the maximum angle to
90 degrees or lower would preserve right angles in the geometry.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of line and polygon features
   :ref:`qgisdensifygeometries`,
   :ref:`qgisdensifygeometriesgivenaninterval`

tools.name: Snap geometries to layer
tools.description:
Snaps the geometries in a layer either to the geometries from
another layer, or to geometries within the same layer.
Matching is done based on a tolerance distance, and vertices will be
inserted or removed as required to make the geometries match the
reference geometries.
:ref:`features in-place modification <processing_inplace_edit>`
of point, line, and polygon features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgissnappointstogrid`

BEHAVIOR.name: BEHAVIOR
BEHAVIOR.description: Snapping can be done to an existing node or a segment (its closest point to the vertex to move). Available snapping options: * 0 --- Prefer aligning nodes, insert extra vertices where required Prefer to snap to nodes, even when a segment may be closer than a node. New nodes will be inserted to make geometries follow each other exactly when inside allowable tolerance. * 1 --- Prefer closest point, insert extra vertices where required Snap to closest point, regardless of it is a node or a segment. New nodes will be inserted to make geometries follow each other exactly when inside allowable tolerance. * 2 --- Prefer aligning nodes, don't insert new vertices Prefer to snap to nodes, even when a segment may be closer than a node. No new nodes will be inserted. * 3 --- Prefer closest point, don't insert new vertices Snap to closest point, regardless of it is a node or a segment. No new nodes will be inserted. * 4 --- Move end points only, prefer aligning nodes Only snap start/end points of lines (point features will also be snapped, polygon features will not be modified), prefer to snap to nodes. * 5 --- Move end points only, prefer closest point Only snap start/end points of lines (point features will also be snapped, polygon features will not be modified), snap to closest point * 6 --- Snap end points to end points only Only snap the start/end points of lines to other start/end points of lines * 7 --- Snap to anchor nodes (single layer only)

discription:
This toolbox is a core collection focused on **spatial relationship assessment and geometric Boolean operations** for vector features. It provides the most fundamental overlay operations in GIS, used to analyze and create **intersection, union, difference, and symmetrical difference** between features, serving as the basis for area delineation, data clipping, and spatial statistical aggregation.

**Core Capabilities (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Clipping & Extraction:** Use the **Clip** tool for precise **polygonal clipping**; or use **Extract by extent** to extract a feature subset by a **rectangular boundary**.
- **Boolean Intersection:** Executes the **Intersection** operation to extract the **common overlapping area** between the input and overlay layers, inheriting all attributes.
- **Boolean Difference:** Executes the **Difference** operation to remove the portion of the input layer that overlaps with the overlay layer; **Symmetrical difference** removes the overlapping area between two layers, preserving all non-overlapping regions.
- **Boolean Union:** Executes the **Union** operation to combine all geometries from both the input and overlay layers, creating new polygons for all resulting spatial partitions.
- **Auxiliary Operations:** **Split with lines** splits features using lines as cutting boundaries; **Line intersections** creates point features at the intersection of lines.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Environmental Assessment:** Use **Intersection** to extract the overlap between a protected area and a road buffer to assess potential impact.
- **Data Cleaning:** Use **Difference** to remove a small developed area from a larger polygon feature.
- **Area Combination:** Use **Union** to merge two adjacent but partially overlapping administrative boundary layers into one complete area analysis layer.

**Tags:**
Overlay Analysis, Boolean Operation, Clip, Intersection, Union, Difference, Symmetrical Difference

tools.name: Clip
tools.description:
Clips a vector layer using the features of an additional polygon
layer.
Only the parts of the features in the input layer that fall within the
polygons of the overlay layer will be added to the resulting layer.
.. include:: ../algs_include.rst
   :start-after: **warning_attributes**
   :end-before: **end_warning_attributes**
This algorithm uses spatial indexes on the providers, prepared
geometries and apply a clipping operation if the geometry isn't wholly
contained by the mask geometry.
  Clipping operation between a two-feature input layer 'a' and a single
  feature overlay layer 'b' (left) - resulting in a new layer with the modified 
  'a' features (right)
of point, line, and polygon features
.. seealso:: :ref:`qgisintersection`, :ref:`qgisdifference`

INPUT.name: INPUT
INPUT.description: Layer containing the features to be clipped

OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Specify the layer to contain the features from the input layer that are inside the overlay (clipping) layer. One of: .. include:: ../algs_include.rst :start-after: **layer_output_types** :end-before: **end_layer_output_types**

OUTPUT.label: Clipped
OUTPUT.name: OUTPUT
OUTPUT.description: Layer containing features from the input layer split by the overlay layer.

tools.name: Difference
tools.description:
Extracts features from the input layer that don't fall within the
boundaries of the overlay layer.
Input layer features that partially overlap the overlay layer
feature(s) are split along the boundary of those feature(s) and only
the portions outside the overlay layer features are retained.

tools.name: Union
tools.description:
Checks overlaps between features within the input layer and creates
separate features for overlapping and non-overlapping parts.
The area of overlap will create as many identical overlapping features
as there are features that participate in that overlap.
  Union operation with a single input layer with two overlapping
  features (left) - resulting in four features (middle) - features moved for clarity (right)
An overlay layer can also be used, in which case features from each
layer are split at their overlap with features from the other one,
creating a layer containing all the portions from both input and
overlay layers. Features on the same layer will not split each other.
The attribute table of the union layer is filled with attribute values
from the respective original layer for non-overlapping features, and
attribute values from both layers for overlapping features.
  Union operation between a two-feature input layer 'a' and a single
  feature overlay layer 'b' (left) - resulting five-feature layer 
  with attributes from both layers (right)
.. note::
   With an overlay layer, features on the same layer will not split each other.
   If you want to split overlaps on the same layer as well as other layers,
   first run the algorithm with multiple layers then run the algorithm
   again with only the previous output.
   :ref:`qgisintersection`

discription:
This toolbox specializes in **data filtering, subset extraction, and random sampling** of vector layers. It provides multiple selection mechanisms based on **attribute value, expression, spatial location, and random methods** to create specific feature collections or sample data required for analysis.

**Core Capabilities (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Select & Extract (Non-Spatial):** Offers **Select/Extract by attribute** and **Select/Extract by expression** for data filtering based on attribute values or complex QGIS expressions. Extract operations output matching and non-matching features as separate layers.
- **Spatial Select & Extract:** Uses **Select/Extract by location** for spatial filtering based on geometric relationships (e.g., intersects, contains); supports **Select/Extract within distance** for proximity extraction based on a **maximum distance threshold**.
- **Random Sampling:** Provides the **Random select/extract** tool series, supporting random sampling **by percentage or count**, and allows for **stratified random sampling** within categories to create statistical samples.
- **Type Filtering:** The **Filter by geometry type** tool separates point, line, and polygon features into different outputs, typically used for flow control in the Modeler.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Target Feature Extraction:** Use **Extract by expression** to extract regions meeting complex attribute criteria (e.g., population > 5000 AND area < 10 sq km).
- **Buffer Analysis:** Use **Select within distance** to find all buildings located within a 100-meter range of a river buffer.
- **Statistical Sampling:** Utilize **Random extract within subsets** to proportionally draw sample points from different land-use types (categories) for stratified random sampling surveys.

**Tags:**
Selection, Extract, Filter, Spatial Relation, Attribute, Expression, Random Sampling, Subset, Distance

discription:
This toolbox specializes in the comprehensive management and modification of a vector layer's **attribute table structure, data types, field content, and calculation**. It is a core toolset for GIS data wrangling, cleaning, and attribute enhancement, used to ensure attribute data integrity and usability.

**Core Capabilities (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Attribute Calculation & Encoding:** Uses **Field calculator** or **Advanced Python field calculator** for complex field assignments; supports adding **Autoincremental field** or **unique value index field** (numerical classification) for unique identification and categorical statistics.
- **Table Structure Refactoring:** The core **Refactor fields** tool supports bulk **modification of field names/types**, **adding/removing fields**, and **reordering**; provides **Drop/Retain fields** and **Rename field** for quick structural adjustments.
- **Geometry Attribute Enhancement:** Uses **Add X Y fields to layer** to save point feature coordinates (X, Y, Z) as new attributes in the table.
- **Data Type & Format Handling:** Supports **Text to float** for data type conversion; can **Extract binary field** contents to files, and **Explode HStore Field** (e.g., OSM tags) into multiple columns.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Data Cleaning:** Use **Refactor fields** to standardize field naming conventions and **Text to float** to convert erroneous text-based numbers to numeric type.
- **Attribute Enhancement:** Add an **Autoincremental field** as a stable ID; use **Field calculator** to compute new statistical values based on existing attributes (e.g., perimeter/area ratio).
- **Coordinate Management:** Use **Add X Y fields to layer** to save the point feature's projected coordinates or lat/lon as attributes for reporting or export.

**Tags:**
Attribute Table, Field Calculator, Structure Management, Data Type, Encoding, Field Refactoring, Coordinate Extraction, Python

tools.name: Add autoincremental field
tools.description:
Adds a new integer field to a vector layer, with a sequential value
for each feature.
This field can be used as a unique ID for features in the layer.
The new attribute is not added to the input layer but a new layer is
generated instead.
The initial starting value for the incremental series can be
specified.
Optionally, the incremental series can be based on grouping fields and
a sort order for features can also be specified.

tools.name: Refactor fields
tools.description:
Allows editing the structure of the attribute table of a vector layer.
Fields can be modified in their type and name, using a fields mapping.
The original layer is not modified. A new layer is generated, which
contains a modified attribute table, according to the provided fields
mapping.
.. note:: When using a template layer with :ref:`constraints <constraints>`
  on fields, the information is displayed in the widget with a coloured
  background and tooltip. Treat this information as a hint during configuration.
  No constraints will be added on an output layer nor will they be checked
  or enforced by the algorithm.
The Refactor fields algorithm allows to:
* Change field names and types
* Add and remove fields
* Reorder fields
* Calculate new fields based on expressions
* Load field list from another layer
  Refactor fields dialog

FIELDS_MAPPING.name: FIELDS_MAPPING
FIELDS_MAPPING.description: List of output fields with their definitions. The embedded table lists all the fields of the source layer and allows you to edit them: * Click to create a new field. * Click to remove a field. * Use and to change the selected field order. * Click to reset to the default view. * Click to invert the selection in the fields list. For each of the fields you'd like to reuse, you need to fill the following options: :guilabel:`Source expression` (``expression``) [expression] Field or expression from the input layer. :guilabel:`Field name` (``name``) [string] Name of the field in the output layer. By default input field name is kept. :guilabel:`Type` (``type``) [enumeration] Data type of the output field. Available types depend on the output layer provider. :guilabel:`Length` (``length``) [number] Length of the output field. :guilabel:`Precision` (``precision``) [number] Precision of the output field. :guilabel:`Constraints` (``constraints``) [string] When using a template layer, indicates whether there are constraints applied to the template field. Hover over the cell to display the constraints. :guilabel:`Field alias` (``field_alias``) [string] Set a name to use as alias for the field. Not supported by all format types. Existing aliases are displayed and will be copied to the destination layer if supported. :guilabel:`Field comment` (``field_comment``) [string] Store a comment describing the field. Not supported by all format types. Existing comments are displayed and will be copied to the destination layer if supported. :guilabel:`Load fields from template layer` Allows to select a layer from the current project as a template and (with :guilabel:`Load fields`) fill the above "Fields mapping" options with its fields and their definitions.

discription:
This toolbox specializes in the reading, writing, and management of the **Vector Tiles** format. It provides core functionality to convert traditional vector layers into an efficient Web map format and to download tiles from online sources, making it essential for achieving **high-performance, small-footprint Web GIS applications**.

**Core Capabilities (Ultimate Concise):**

- **Vector Tile Generation:** Supports exporting one or more vector layers into the Web map optimized vector tile format, with options to output as a **single MBTiles file** or an **XYZ directory structure**.
- **Tile Download:** Uses the **Download vector tiles** tool to download specified extents and zoom levels of tiles from a connected vector tile layer for offline use or local backup.

**Typical Scenarios:**
- **Web Map Publishing:** Use **Write vector tiles (MBTiles)** to export complex road or parcel layers into a single MBTiles file for fast, high-performance rendering in Web frameworks like Leaflet/MapLibre.
- **Offline Data Preparation:** Download high-resolution vector tiles to a local file to serve as an **offline data source** for mobile applications.

**Tags:**
Vector Tiles, MBTiles, XYZ, Web GIS, Offline Map, Data Publishing
